\section{Purpose}

When a formalization relies on a cited mathematical source, the cited source
should remain intact.  It is a source, not an errata file.  If a possible gap,
missing hypothesis, incorrect numerical constant, or other mathematical
discrepancy is found, the matter should be recorded in a separate LaTeX note.
In this repository such notes live under \path{docs/paper-gaps/}.  The same
principle applies when the formal development has already diverged from the
cited source, for instance by changing a statement so that it compiles, or by
using a different mathematical route because an available formal-library theorem
has a slightly different form.  Such a note is a mathematical note first, and a
record of the formalization second: it should be readable by a mathematician or
mathematical physicist who has not followed the issue discussion.

The note should isolate the mathematical mechanism.  It should say what the
cited source asserts, what the cited results actually imply, where a term or
hypothesis is lost, and what statement the formal development proves instead.
If the formal proof takes a different route, the note should explain the
replacement argument and the hypotheses on which it rests.  This is especially
important when the proof uses a theorem, construction, or convention from
Mathlib which is not part of the cited argument.  In that case the note should
state the Mathlib result in ordinary mathematical language, explain how it is
specialized to the notation of the paper, and compare its hypotheses and
conclusion with the step it replaces.  It should not merely say that \Lean{} did
not accept a proof, that the modified proof compiles, or that a named library
lemma was applied.

The documents in this directory should themselves follow this standard.  A
policy or template which reads like a checklist will tend to produce checklist
notes; the examples and templates should therefore be written as mathematical
prose.

\section{Concision and Readability}

A paper-gap note should be short enough that a reader can understand the issue
in one sitting.  The first page should answer four questions: what the source
uses, how hard the remaining formal work is, what the formalization or audit
checked, and what the current verdict is.  Begin with a short
\emph{At a glance} section when the note concerns an open or recently resolved
formalization task.  That section should estimate the difficulty, the rough
implementation weight, the split between Mathlib reuse and project-local work,
and the key Mathlib APIs or modules.  Use honest ranges, not false precision.

The \emph{Key theorem forms} section should be Section~2, immediately after
\emph{At a glance}.  Put the theorem forms before the source details so the
reader knows what the formalization is aiming to prove.  After that, keep the
source assertion, the mechanism being checked, the blueprint/formal comparison,
and the conclusion.  Use more sections only when a counterexample or long
derivation genuinely needs room.

Keep background to the minimum needed for the local point.  Prefer one clear
special case over a general restatement of the surrounding theorem.  Use displayed
equations for the source assertion, the key calculation, and the theorem forms;
avoid displays for traceability data, declaration names, or long lists.  The
blueprint/formal comparison should be compact and should not repeat the theorem
forms.  The section ``Form of the Note'' below specifies where traceability data
belongs; the body should read as mathematical prose, not as a log.

If the verdict is that there is no mathematical discrepancy, say so plainly and
stop.  Keep the conclusion highly compact, normally under twenty source lines.
If the only remaining work is an implementation task, name it briefly and link
the issue or pull request in a footnote.

\section{When the Investigation Starts}

The investigation starts when the obstruction appears to be mathematical rather
than merely formal.  No final judgement is needed at this stage.  It is enough
that, after reading the relevant source and attempting the corresponding formal
statement, the proof seems to require a different scalar, an additional
hypothesis, a different tensor placement, a distinction between two objects which
the prose identifies, or an auxiliary assertion not supplied by the cited
argument.

The same investigation should also start when such a deviation is discovered
after the fact.  If the existing formal development or informal blueprint has
already changed the statement, strengthened a hypothesis, weakened a conclusion,
inserted an unadvertised lemma, or replaced the cited proof by a different
formal-library argument, the mathematical change should be documented even if all
relevant files already compile.

At this early stage the purpose is to preserve the question while it is still
local.  The note may later conclude that the matter is only notational, that an
intermediate estimate in the cited source needs a harmless correction, that a
missing hypothesis is genuinely needed, or that no discrepancy remains.  Thus
the trigger is not the severity of the eventual verdict, but the appearance of a
real mismatch between the cited reasoning and the statement that can be
formalized.

A failed tactic search, a missing formal lemma, or an inconvenient coercion is
not enough.  The obstruction must survive translation back into ordinary
mathematics.

Sometimes an investigation uncovers an improvement that is not a discrepancy:
the formalization works correctly, but it could be simplified by using an
existing library, replacing a custom type, or adopting a cleaner proof route.
These are not, by themselves, paper-gap notes.  They are action items.  When
such an improvement is identified, open a GitHub issue or pull request that
describes the proposed change.  If the investigation also produces a paper-gap
note, link the issue or pull request from that note: the note records the
mathematical justification, and the issue or pull request drives the
implementation.

\section{When to Write a Note}

A note should be written once the source argument and the formal proof no longer
match as mathematical arguments.  This includes, for instance, a numerical
estimate whose constant does not follow from the cited lemma, a displayed
conclusion which uses an unstated hypothesis, or a step in which two objects are
identified although they must remain distinct.  In analytic, algebraic,
probabilistic, or quantum arguments, such distinctions may concern the domain of
a map, the placement of a tensor factor, the type of an outcome, the distinction
between a structure and a substructure, or the scalar carried by an approximation
relation.

A note is required when an audit finds that a Lean declaration associated with a
source-labelled statement has acquired an extra non-source hypothesis, such as
bridge, residual, repair, producer, or obligation-structure data.  Such a
declaration is temporary proof debt, not a replacement for the source theorem,
and should not be introduced merely to avoid a \verb|sorry|.  The note must say
plainly that the Lean result is conditional, identify the source-faithful theorem
form that remains to be proved, and give the intended obligation discharger or
removal plan.  The blueprint should not mark the source-labelled statement with
\verb|\leanok| by pointing to this conditional helper.

Changing a Lean theorem away from the statement in
\path{references/ldt-paper/} is strongly discouraged.  A paper-gap note should
not make such a change look routine: it should explain the mathematical
necessity, or else classify the change as proof debt to be removed.

When an existing conditional helper is audited, the first task is to extract any
argument it already contains into source-faithful lemmas.  If the remaining
bridge hypothesis cannot be derived from the paper hypotheses, the formal
development should restore the source theorem statement and record the missing
proof obligation explicitly, rather than retaining the strengthened statement as
though it were the paper theorem.

This requirement is not meant to classify every explicit Lean side condition as
a discrepancy.  Positivity, nonemptiness, decidability, field-model instances,
and denominator nonvanishing hypotheses may be faithful encodings of the domain
in which the paper's theorem is stated.  The note should distinguish such
boundary hypotheses from hypotheses that supply an unproved step of the paper
argument.

A note is also appropriate when the proof becomes formal only after changing an
intermediate scalar, weakening a conclusion, strengthening a hypothesis, or
inserting an additional lemma which is not simply an expansion of the cited
argument.  These are mathematical changes, even when they are harmless for the
final theorem.  It is likewise appropriate when an available formal-library
theorem proves the needed result under a somewhat different formulation from the
cited source.  In that case the note should be deliberately pedagogical.  It
should explain, in ordinary mathematical language, what the replacement result
says, how it is specialized, which hypotheses are new or differently packaged,
and why the resulting statement is a legitimate substitute for the step in the
cited argument.  If the issue remains open after reasonable attempts, the note
should say what has been checked and what remains unknown.

\section{Counterexamples}

If the cited assertion appears to be false, the note should not stop at saying
that the proof cannot be formalized.  It should give the counterexample, or the
smallest relevant part of it, in ordinary mathematical notation.  The example
should be accompanied by enough verification that the reader can see both sides:
the hypotheses of the cited assertion hold, and its conclusion fails.

When feasible, the counterexample should also be formalized in \Lean{}.  This is
especially valuable when the example is finite, algebraic, computational, or
otherwise small enough that the failure can be checked without reproducing the
whole surrounding theory.  The note should then state the mathematical content
of the checked counterexample and identify the corresponding Lean declaration in
a footnote.  The Lean file is not a substitute for the prose: the prose should
still explain why the example refutes the cited assertion.

\section{Revision of a Note}

A paper-gap note may be provisional.  It may begin as soon as the mathematical
obstruction has been isolated well enough to state the question, and it may be
revised as the calculation, the blueprint, or the corresponding \Lean{}
declarations become clearer.  The first version need not know the final
classification, but it should say plainly which mathematical point is known and
which point remains unsettled.

Later revisions should not make the note into a chronological log.  They should
rewrite the document so that it remains a coherent account of the present
mathematical understanding.  If the verdict changes, the conclusion should state
the current verdict; the linked issue or pull request can preserve the earlier
discussion.

\section{Form of the Note}

Each note should stand on its own.  It should give the date, cite the relevant
source article, and provide enough traceability for the reader to locate the
original passage and the project discussion.  GitHub issues and pull requests may
be linked with \verb|\href|, and source files, line ranges, and labels should be
recorded when they help the reader check the claim.  These references should
serve the exposition rather than govern it: the main text should be organized
around the mathematical assertion and its proof.

The note should introduce its notation before using it.  Symbols for
measurements, tensor factors, approximation relations, and error parameters
should be named in prose.  If an approximation relation is state-dependent, the
state should be named, or its defining expression should be given when this can
be done briefly.  Only after the notation is in place should the note state the
assertion in the cited source, using a bibliographic citation such as
\verb|\cite[Section~...]{...}| when the section or chapter is known.

Only the relevant hypotheses should be reproduced.  If the question is a scalar
substitution, a missing term, or a missing hypothesis, the note should not quote
a long unrelated part of the proof.  It should give the cited lemma or
proposition in the special case actually used, then display the calculation or
logical implication in which the discrepancy appears.

Displayed equations should be used with restraint.  They are appropriate for the
source estimate being checked, the cited estimate in the form actually used, and
the calculation where a term or hypothesis appears or disappears.  When a
displayed equation is identified by a source label, the label should appear on
the right of the display, while the surrounding prose refers to the mathematical
assertion itself.  The standard \texttt{amsmath} command \verb|\tag| is the
right mechanism for this; a separate local convention should be introduced only
if the standard mechanism is genuinely insufficient.  For a multi-line aligned
display, tag the individual lines that carry the source information rather than
forcing a long combined label below the equations.  Short
scalar definitions and elementary inequalities should remain inline when the
sentence reads better that way.  As in ordinary mathematical writing, a displayed
formula is part of the surrounding sentence and should be punctuated accordingly.

Bibliographic entries used only by these notes should live in
\path{docs/paper-gaps/references.bib}.  A new note should ordinarily begin from
\path{docs/paper-gaps/template.tex}, which records the common LaTeX preamble,
the local bibliography, and a model for right-hand source labels in displayed
equations.

Blueprint prose cites a note like any other source, with
\verb|\cite{gap:<slug>}|; the bibliography entry in
\path{blueprint/src/references.bib} carries the published URL of the note,
whether the note lives in this repository or in another one.  Lean docstrings
and comments use the repository path form \path{docs/paper-gaps/<slug>.tex}.

The note should then compare the cited source with the informal blueprint, if
there is one, and with the formal statement.  This comparison should be written
in ordinary mathematical prose.  Formal declaration names and source paths should
be supplied only to identify the exact formal statements, and normally belong in
footnotes.

The conclusion should give a verdict.  It may say that there is no discrepancy,

\section{At a glance}

\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Difficulty: medium.}  Two related matters are recorded.
  First, the soundness analysis of the Pauli basis test invokes the
  classical low individual degree game at dimension $2m+2$, and the game's
  question distribution is undefined at that dimension for the admissible
  parameters: it requires $2m+2$ to divide $q$, while admissibility supplies
  only $m \mid q$; the repair is a statement-level reformulation of an
  imported theorem, not a new proof.  Second, the import of the classical
  game's quantum soundness from the tensor-code paper carries two open
  verification obligations at every dimension: the asserted identity with
  the cited tensor-code test is not an identity and must be replaced by a
  reduction with a value bound, and the source's instantiation of the
  theorem's auxiliary parameter violates its lower bound at small
  dimensions (Section~\ref{sec:import-obligations}).
  \item \textbf{Estimated weight:} for the recommended direction, about
  \textbf{3--5 new definitions or interfaces} (a line-point distribution with

  including the strategy-transport layer between the directly indexed game
  and the $\chi$-based game (parsing pullback, seed-fiber averaging with

  trip of the soundness conclusion); several hundred lines of formal proof.

  Section~\ref{sec:import-obligations} adds the pair-measurement

  \item \textbf{Key Mathlib inputs:} uniform distributions on finite types

\section{Key theorem forms}

Throughout, $q = 2^k$ with $k$ odd is an admissible field size, the tuple
$(q,m,d)$ is admissible when moreover $d \ge 1$ and $m \mid q$, and
$\mathrm{ideg}_{d,m}(\F_q)$ denotes the $m$-variate polynomial representatives
over $\F_q$ of individual degree at most $d$.  The comparison involves four
theorem forms.
\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{Source theorem form} (the polynomial-pair measurement).  There
  is a function $\delta_S(\eps,m,d,q) = a(md)^a(\eps^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bmd})$,
  for universal constants $a > 1$ and $0 < b < 1$, such that for every
  admissible $(q,m,d)$ and every projective strategy for the Pauli basis test
  succeeding with probability at least $1-\eps$, there is a projective
  measurement $\{\hat S_{g_X,g_Z}\}$ with outcomes pairs of polynomials in
  $\mathrm{ideg}_{d,m}(\F_q)$ whose evaluations are $\delta_S$-consistent, on
  average over a uniform point $u \in \F_q^m$ and in both bases
  $W \in \{X,Z\}$, with the corresponding points measurements
  $\{\hat M^{(\mathrm{Point},W),u}_a\}$ of the strategy, together with the
  symmetric counterpart of this relation.
  \item \textbf{Missing instantiation obligation.}  The classical low
  individual degree game with parameter tuple $(q,\, 2m+2,\, d,\, 1)$ is well
  defined, and the combined point and line measurements assembled in the
  analysis constitute a strategy for it of value at least
  $1 - \delta_{\mathrm{combine}}$.  The game's question distribution draws
  its axis and diagonal indices through an index function
  $\chi_{2m+2}\colon \F_q \to \{1,\ldots,2m+2\}$ with classes of equal size
  $q/(2m+2)$, so the game exists only when $2m+2$ divides $q$.
  \item \textbf{Restricted form supported by the present route.}  The source
  theorem form under the additional hypothesis $2m+2 \mid q$.  Among
  admissible tuples this hypothesis holds exactly when $m = 1$ and
  $q \ge 8$; it fails for every admissible tuple with $m \ge 2$ and for
  $(q,m) = (2,1)$.
  \item \textbf{Repaired import form} (recommended target).  Quantum
  soundness of the directly indexed variant of the classical low individual
  degree game over $\F_q^{m'}$, for every dimension $m' \ge 1$ and
  admissible $q$, with no divisibility hypothesis: the question
  distribution samples the axis index, and the diagonal prefix index,
  uniformly from $\{1,\ldots,m'\}$ directly rather than through an index
  function on $\F_q$, and line questions carry the sampled index itself in
  place of the seed $s \in \F_q$; the error is
  $\delta_{\mathrm{ld}}(\eps,q,m',d,k) = a(dm'k)^a(\eps^b + q^{-b} +
  2^{-bm'd})$.  This is a candidate target form, not an established one:
  proving it carries the same two import obligations as the $\chi$-based
  import (Section~\ref{sec:import-obligations}), and deriving the present
  form from it when $m' \mid q$ requires the strategy transport described
  under the candidate repairs below, whose synchronicity step is an open
  obligation.
\end{enumerate}

\section{The source assertion and the obstruction}

We examine the final step of the subsection ``Applying the classical
low-degree test'' in the analysis of the Pauli basis test in the compression
paper of Ji, Natarajan, Vidick, Wright, and Yuen (MIP$^{*}$=RE,
arXiv:2001.04383), whose quantum soundness component builds on the low
individual degree test of \cite{Ji2020LowIndividualDegree}.%
\footnote{Tracked in \localissue{0002}.  In the mirror of the source
consulted here, the polynomial-pair lemma and its proof are at
\path{references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex},
lines~1267--1288; the sub-line lemma is at lines~1063--1116 and the combined
line lemma at lines~1020--1034 of the same file.  The game parametrization
with its divisibility, the index function, the soundness statement with its
proof, and admissibility are at
\path{references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex},
lines~33--35, 214--219, 413--458, and 958--961.}
There, the combined point measurements
$\{\hat Q^{x,z,\alpha,\beta}_c\}$ and combined line measurements
$\{\hat Q^{\ell}_f\}$, indexed by points of $\F_q^{2m+2}$ and lines in
$\F_q^{2m+2}$, are asserted to form a strategy for the classical low
individual degree game with parameters
\[
  \mathsf{ldparams} = (q,\, 2m+2,\, d,\, 1)
  \tag{\path{lem:qld-4-7}}
\]
of value $1 - \delta_{\mathrm{combine}}$, and the quantum soundness theorem
for that game is applied to produce the global polynomial-pair measurement.
The two lemmas feeding this step are stated for the line-point distribution
over $\F_q^{2m+2}$.

The game, however, is parametrized by tuples $(q,m',d,k)$ with $q$ an
admissible field size \emph{and $m'$ dividing $q$}.  The divisibility is not
incidental: the question distribution is a conditionally linear distribution
in which a uniform seed coordinate $s \in \F_q$, read as an integer in
$\{0,\ldots,q-1\}$, determines the axis or diagonal index through the unique
$\chi(s)$ with
\[
  s = (\chi(s)-1)\,\frac{q}{m'} + r, \qquad 0 \le r < \frac{q}{m'},
  \tag{\path{eq:chi-func}}
\]
so that the $m'$ classes $\chi^{-1}(i)$ partition $\F_q$ into sets of equal
size $q/m'$ and the index is uniform.  For $m' \nmid q$ neither the index
function nor the line-point distribution built from it is defined.

Admissibility of $(q,m,d)$ supplies only $m \mid q$.  Since an admissible $q$
is a power of two, $m \mid q$ forces $m = 2^j$.  For $j \ge 1$ the integer
$m+1 \ge 3$ is odd, so $2m+2 = 2(m+1)$ has an odd factor exceeding $1$ and
divides no power of two; for $m = 1$ the condition $4 \mid q$ holds for every
admissible $q$ except $q = 2$.  Thus the instantiation at dimension $2m+2$ is
undefined for every admissible tuple with $m \ge 2$: for instance
$(q,m,d) = (8,2,1)$ is admissible, while $6 \nmid 8$.  The source performs
the instantiation without addressing the divisibility, so its proof route
establishes the polynomial-pair lemma, and with it the soundness theorem for
the Pauli basis test that rests on it, only for $m = 1$ and $q \ge 8$.

\section{What the cited soundness theorem requires: the import obligations}
\label{sec:import-obligations}

The quantum soundness theorem for the classical game inherits the constraint
$m' \mid q$ solely because it is stated for the game just described; its
proof fixes an admissible $q$ with $m' \mid q$, asserts that the game with
simultaneity parameter $1$ is \emph{identical} to the two-prover tensor-code
test for the Reed--Solomon tensor code $\mathcal C^{\ot m'}$ of the same
authors' \emph{Quantum soundness of testing tensor codes} (arXiv:2111.08131)
\cite{Ji2021Quantum}, and concludes by Theorem~4.7 there, instantiated with
that theorem's auxiliary integer parameter --- denoted $k$ in that source,
and written $K$ here to avoid clashing with the field exponent and the
simultaneity parameter --- chosen as $(m')^3 d$.  Neither
the asserted identity nor the instantiation is complete as stated, so the
import carries two verification obligations, which this section details and
which the blueprint's proof node for the soundness statement records as
open.  Both obligations are independent of the divisibility question: they
arise at every dimension, for the $\chi$-based game where it is defined and
equally for the directly indexed variant proposed under the candidate
repairs.

\paragraph{The cited test.}
In the two-prover tensor-code test (Figures~1 and~2 of
\cite{Ji2021Quantum}; the two-prover strategy format and the goodness
measure are Definitions~4.5 and~4.6 there), the referee performs one of
three subtests with probability $1/3$ each, assigning the two roles of each
subtest to the two provers uniformly at random.  \emph{Axis-parallel lines
test}: sample a uniform point $u \in [n]^{m'}$ and a uniform axis
$j \in \{1,\ldots,m'\}$; send the axis-parallel line $\ell$ through $u$ in
direction $j$ to one prover, who answers a codeword $g \in \mathcal C$;
send $u$ to the other, who answers a field value $a$; accept iff
$g(u_j) = a$.  \emph{Subcube commutation test}: sample
$j \in \{1,\ldots,m'\}$ and a subcube $H \subseteq [n]^{m'}$ by fixing the
last $j-1$ coordinates uniformly; sample $u, v$ independently and uniformly
in $H$ and a uniform order bit; send the ordered pair $(u,v)$ or $(v,u)$ to
one prover, who answers a pair $(b_u, b_v)$ of field values; send $u$ to
the other, who answers $a$; accept iff $b_u = a$.  \emph{Synchronicity
test}: send one identical question --- a line, a point, or an ordered
pair, with probability $1/3$ each --- to both provers and accept iff their
answers agree.  Theorem~4.7 supposes a two-prover strategy passing this
test with probability $1-\eps$ together with an integer parameter
$K \ge 12 m' t$, where $t$ is the interpolation parameter of the base code
--- for the degree-$d$ Reed--Solomon code, of blocklength $n = q$ and
distance $q-d$, one has $t = d+1$ --- and produces projective measurements
$\{G_c\}$ and $\{\tilde G_c\}$ with outcomes in $\mathcal C^{\ot m'}$,
consistent with one prover's points measurements, with the other prover's
lines measurements, and with each other, up to
$\eta'(m',t,K,\eps,n^{-1}) = \mathrm{poly}(m',t,K) \cdot
\mathrm{poly}(\eps, n^{-1}, e^{-K/(m')^2})$.

\paragraph{Obligation 1: the game correspondence.}
The source asserts that the $\chi$-based game at parameters $(q,m',d,1)$
is this test.  It is not, in four respects.
(i)~The game has no pair questions.  A pair question of the test reveals
two points of a \emph{hidden} subcube --- the subcube itself is not sent
--- and is answered by two field values, while the game's diagonal-line
question reveals a full line description and is answered by a degree-$m'd$
polynomial.  A reduction must construct the pair measurements from the
diagonal-line measurements by post-processing (measure a line through $u$
and $v$ and evaluate the answered polynomial at the two parameters), and
both directions of the information mismatch matter: the game's line
description carries an index and a seed, neither of which is a function of
the pair $(u,v)$, so the constructed measurement must average over the
compatible indices and seeds; and the game's diagonal lines fix the
\emph{first} $i-1$ coordinates where the test's subcubes fix the
\emph{last} $j-1$, so the coordinate conventions must be aligned.  The
construction must preserve projectivity and must match the law of the
hidden-subcube pair with the law induced by the game's diagonal sampling.
(ii)~The game's line questions carry the seed $s \in \F_q$; the test's
carry only the line.  A strategy may depend on the seed beyond its class
$\chi^{-1}(i)$, and removing this dependence runs into the fiber-averaging
difficulty made explicit under the candidate repairs: averaging preserves
the line-versus-point branches exactly but not the synchronicity branches.
(iii)~The branch weights differ: each nontrivial cross-test has mass $1/3$
in the test against $2/9$ in the game.  Once the per-branch predicates are
matched, the intended bookkeeping bound is that the constructed strategy's
rejection probability in the test is at most $\tfrac32$ times the game's
rejection probability, up to the $O(1/(m'q))$ of item~(iv); this bound is
the target of the obligation, not an established fact.
(iv)~The game's predicate fixes an acceptance convention on diagonal
questions with zero direction --- an event of probability at most
$2/(m'q)$, recorded in the blueprint's remark on zero directions --- for
which the test has no counterpart branch.
Finally, the displayed conclusions of Theorem~4.7 pair one prover's points
measurements with the other prover's tensor-codeword measurement, and the
first prover's tensor-codeword measurement with the second prover's lines
measurements, while the game-level statement asserts the point consistency
in both directions; deriving the stated form uses the role symmetrization
of the test and belongs to the correspondence.  None of these steps is
difficult to state, but none is carried out in the source, and together
they replace the asserted one-line identity by a reduction carrying its
own value bound.

\paragraph{Obligation 2: the parameter bound.}
Theorem~4.7 requires $K \ge 12 m' t = 12 m' (d+1)$.  The source
instantiates $K = (m')^3 d$, which meets the bound iff
$(m')^2 d \ge 12(d+1)$: this holds for all $d \ge 1$ when $m' \ge 5$,
holds at $m' = 4$ exactly when $d \ge 3$, and fails for every $d$ when
$m' \le 3$.  In the game's parameter domain the dimension divides the
admissible field size and is therefore a power of two, so the source's
instantiation violates the hypothesis exactly at $m' \in \{1,2\}$ for
every $d$ and at $m' = 4$ for $d \in \{1,2\}$ --- in particular, in the
multilinear regime $d = 1$, at every dimension $m' \le 4$.  A candidate
repair is to instantiate $K = \max((m')^3 d,\, 12 m'(d+1))$; the open
obligation is then to re-absorb the error, that is, to check that
$\mathrm{poly}(m',t,K)$ and $e^{-K/(m')^2}$ still collapse to the form
$a(dm')^a(\eps^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bm'd})$ in the small-$m'$ cases where the
maximum is $12m'(d+1)$ --- plausible, since there
$e^{-K/(m')^2} = e^{-12(d+1)/m'}$ decays in $d$ at a rate comparable to
$2^{-m'd}$ for $m' \le 4$, but not checked here.

In the correspondence of Obligation~1, the only role of the divisibility
$m' \mid q$ is to make the $\chi$-sampled index uniform.  The underlying
mathematics does not need the divisibility.  The low
individual degree test of \cite{Ji2020LowIndividualDegree} samples its axis
index $i$ uniformly from $\{1,\ldots,m'\}$ directly, with no index function
on $\F_q$ and no divisibility hypothesis,%
\footnote{See the test figure in \path{references/ldt-paper/test_definition.tex}.}
and the tensor-code test is likewise a test about the code
$\mathcal C^{\ot m'}$, not about an encoding of indices into $\F_q$.  The
$\chi$-based packaging exists so that the question distribution is
conditionally linear, which the introspection machinery requires for the
game the players actually play --- the Pauli basis test at dimension $m$,
where admissibility does supply the divisibility.  The game at dimension
$2m+2$ never appears in a verifier; it is an internal analysis device in the
proof of the polynomial-pair lemma, so nothing there requires its question
distribution to be conditionally linear.

    60	    (mu : Distribution X) (e : Beta ≃ Alpha)
    61	    (A B : X → Alpha → Op iota) (psi : EuclideanSpace ℂ iota) :
    62	    consistencyDefect mu
    63	        (fun x b => A x (e b)) (fun x b => B x (e b)) psi =
    64	      consistencyDefect mu A B psi := by
    65	  unfold consistencyDefect
    66	  apply avgOver_congr
    67	  intro x
    68	  let term : Alpha → Alpha → ℝ := fun a b =>
    69	    if a = b then 0 else
    70	      (inner ℂ psi ((EuclideanSpace.equiv iota ℂ).symm
    71	        (((A x a) * (B x b)).mulVec psi))).re
    72	  calc
    73	    _ = ∑ a : Beta, ∑ b : Beta, term (e a) (e b) := by
    74	      apply Finset.sum_congr rfl
    75	      intro a _
    76	      apply Finset.sum_congr rfl
    77	      intro b _
    78	      unfold term
    79	      by_cases hab : a = b
    80	      · subst b
    81	        simp
    82	      · have heab : e a ≠ e b := fun h => hab (e.injective h)
    83	        simp [hab, heab]
    84	    _ =
    85	        ∑ a : Beta, ∑ b : Alpha, term (e a) b := by
    86	      apply Finset.sum_congr rfl
    87	      intro a _
    88	      exact Equiv.sum_comp e (fun b => term (e a) b)
    89	    _ = ∑ a : Alpha, ∑ b : Alpha, term a b :=
    90	      Equiv.sum_comp e (fun a => ∑ b : Alpha, term a b)
    91	    _ = _ := rfl
    92	
    93	/-- Simultaneous bijective relabeling of uniform questions and outcomes leaves
    94	the consistency defect unchanged. -/
    95	theorem consistencyDefect_uniform_question_outcome_equiv
    96	    {X Y Alpha Beta iota : Type*}
    97	    [Fintype X] [DecidableEq X] [Nonempty X]
    98	    [Fintype Y] [DecidableEq Y] [Nonempty Y]
    99	    [Fintype Alpha] [DecidableEq Alpha]
   100	    [Fintype Beta] [DecidableEq Beta]
   101	    [Fintype iota] [DecidableEq iota]
   102	    (questionEquiv : X ≃ Y) (outcomeEquiv : Beta ≃ Alpha)
   103	    (A B : Y → Alpha → Op iota) (psi : EuclideanSpace ℂ iota) :
   104	    consistencyDefect (uniformDistribution X)
   105	        (fun x b => A (questionEquiv x) (outcomeEquiv b))
   106	        (fun x b => B (questionEquiv x) (outcomeEquiv b)) psi =
   107	      consistencyDefect (uniformDistribution Y) A B psi := by
   108	  calc
   109	    consistencyDefect (uniformDistribution X)
   110	        (fun x b => A (questionEquiv x) (outcomeEquiv b))
   111	        (fun x b => B (questionEquiv x) (outcomeEquiv b)) psi =
   112	      consistencyDefect (uniformDistribution X)
   113	        (fun x a => A (questionEquiv x) a)
   114	        (fun x a => B (questionEquiv x) a) psi :=
   115	      consistencyDefect_outcome_equiv (uniformDistribution X)
   116	        outcomeEquiv _ _ psi
   117	    _ = consistencyDefect (uniformDistribution Y) A B psi :=
   118	      consistencyDefect_uniform_question_equiv questionEquiv A B psi
   119	
   120	/-- Pointwise equality of both operator families gives equality of their
   121	consistency defects. -/
   122	theorem consistencyDefect_congr
   123	    {X Outcome iota : Type*}
   124	    [Fintype X] [DecidableEq X]
   125	    [Fintype Outcome] [DecidableEq Outcome]
   126	    [Fintype iota] [DecidableEq iota]
   127	    (mu : Distribution X) (A A' B B' : X → Outcome → Op iota)
   128	    (psi : EuclideanSpace ℂ iota)
   129	    (hA : ∀ x a, A x a = A' x a) (hB : ∀ x a, B x a = B' x a) :
   130	    consistencyDefect mu A B psi = consistencyDefect mu A' B' psi := by
   131	  unfold consistencyDefect
   132	  apply avgOver_congr
   133	  intro x
   134	  apply Finset.sum_congr rfl
   135	  intro a _
   136	  apply Finset.sum_congr rfl
   137	  intro b _
   138	  by_cases hab : a = b
   139	  · simp [hab]
   140	  · simp only [hab, if_false]
   141	    rw [hA x a, hB x b]
   142	
   143	/-- The quantitative relation in `def:consistency`, blueprint
   144	`ch12_qpbt_games.tex:195-208`, paper `06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:232-248`. -/
   145	def IsConsistentWithin {X α ι : Type*}
   146	    [Fintype X] [DecidableEq X] [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α]
   147	    [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
   148	    (μ : Distribution X) (A B : X → α → Op ι)
   149	    (ψ : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι) (δ : ℝ) : Prop :=
   150	  consistencyDefect μ A B ψ ≤ δ
   151	
   152	/-- Unit-alphabet specialization of `def:povm-distance`, blueprint
   153	`ch12_qpbt_games.tex:219-226`, paper `06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:258-271`. -/
   154	noncomputable def opDistSq {X ι : Type*}
   155	    [Fintype X] [DecidableEq X] [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
   156	    (μ : Distribution X) (M N : X → Op ι) (ψ : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι) : ℝ :=
   157	  opFamilyDistSq μ (fun x (_ : Unit) => M x) (fun x (_ : Unit) => N x) ψ
   158

   160	`def:povm-distance`, blueprint `ch12_qpbt_games.tex:219-226`, paper
   161	`06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:258-271`. -/
   162	theorem opDistSq_eq_opFamilyDistSq {X ι : Type*}
   163	    [Fintype X] [DecidableEq X] [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
   164	    (μ : Distribution X) (M N : X → Op ι) (ψ : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι) :
   165	    opDistSq μ M N ψ = opFamilyDistSq μ (fun x (_ : Unit) => M x)
   166	      (fun x (_ : Unit) => N x) ψ := rfl
   167	
   168	/-- The strategy-distance relation `def:strategy-distance`. The two strategies'
   169	local Hilbert spaces are identified, and both measurement distances are
   170	evaluated on the first strategy's state. Blueprint
   171	`ch12_qpbt_games.tex:228-237`, paper `06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:273-285`. -/
   172	structure AreCloseStrategies (G : Game) (S S' : Strategy G) (δ : ℝ) : Prop where
   173	  /-- Identification of Alice's local Hilbert spaces. -/
   174	  hA : S.ιA = S'.ιA
   175	  /-- Identification of Bob's local Hilbert spaces. -/
   176	  hB : S.ιB = S'.ιB
   177	  state : stateDistSq S.ψ (reindexState
   178	      (Equiv.prodCongr (Equiv.cast hA).symm (Equiv.cast hB).symm) S'.ψ) ≤ δ
   179	  alice : opFamilyDistSq (G.μ.map Prod.fst)
   180	      (fun x a => heteroKron ((S.A x).effect a) 1)
   181	      (fun x a => heteroKron (reindexOp (Equiv.cast hA) ((S'.A x).effect a)) 1)
   182	      S.ψ ≤ δ
   183	  bob : opFamilyDistSq (G.μ.map Prod.snd)
   184	      (fun y b => heteroKron 1 ((S.B y).effect b))
   185	      (fun y b => heteroKron 1 (reindexOp (Equiv.cast hB) ((S'.B y).effect b)))
   186	      S.ψ ≤ δ
   187	
   188	end MIPStarRE.QPBT
     1	import MIPStarRE.Quantum.FiniteMatrix.NormalizedTrace
     2	
     3	/-!
     4	# Matrix-valued measurements for the MIP*=RE project
     5	
     6	This file provides the matrix-valued measurement layer used by the LDT formalization.
     7	
     8	## Main definitions
     9	
    10	* `Submeasurement` — a family of PSD matrices summing to at most the identity.
    11	* `Measurement` — a family of PSD matrices summing to exactly the identity.
    12	* `Submeasurement.postprocess` — data-processed submeasurements via answer relabeling.
    13	* `Measurement.postprocess` — the paper's postprocessing proposition for complete POVMs.
    14	* `inconsistency` — the off-diagonal mass `∑_{a ≠ b} τ(M_a N_b)`.
    15	* `diagOverlap` — the diagonal mass `∑_a τ(M_a N_a)`.
    16	
    17	## References
    18	
    19	This file builds the project's finite-dimensional measurement layer on top of
    20	the normalized-trace and positive-operator facts in `MIPStarRE.Quantum.FiniteMatrix`
    21	for the quantum formalization in `references/ldt-paper/`.
    22	-/
    23	
    24	open scoped BigOperators MatrixOrder Matrix ComplexOrder
    25	
    26	namespace MIPStarRE.Quantum
    27	
    28	/-! ## Submeasurements and measurements -/
    29	
    30	/--
    31	A submeasurement on a finite answer type `α` is a family of PSD matrices
    32	`M : α → Op d` with `∑ a, M a ≤ 1`.
    33	-/
    34	structure Submeasurement (α : Type*) [Fintype α] (d : Type*) [Fintype d] [DecidableEq d] where
    35	  /-- The effect operators. -/
    36	  effect : α → Op d
    37	  /-- Each effect is positive semidefinite. -/
    38	  pos : ∀ a, 0 ≤ effect a
    39	  /-- The effects sum to at most the identity. -/
    40	  sum_le_one : ∑ a, effect a ≤ 1
    41	
    42	/--
    43	A measurement is a submeasurement whose effects sum exactly to the identity.
    44	-/
    45	structure Measurement (α : Type*) [Fintype α] (d : Type*) [Fintype d] [DecidableEq d]
    46	    extends Submeasurement α d where
    47	  /-- The effects sum to the identity. -/
    48	  sum_eq_one : ∑ a, effect a = 1
    49	
    50	/-! ## Totals and postprocessing -/
    51	
    52	namespace Submeasurement
    53	
    54	variable {d : Type*} [Fintype d] [DecidableEq d]
    55	variable {α β : Type*} [Fintype α] [Fintype β]
    56	
    57	/-! ### Totals and postprocessing -/
    58	
    59	/-- The total operator `∑ a, M_a`. -/
    60	noncomputable def total (M : Submeasurement α d) : Op d :=
    61	  ∑ a, M.effect a
    62	
    63	/--
    64	Data processing: relabel the answer set by `f : α → β`, summing the effects over
    65	fibers.
    66	-/
    67	noncomputable def postprocess [DecidableEq α] [DecidableEq β]
    68	    (M : Submeasurement α d) (f : α → β) : Submeasurement β d where
    69	  effect b := ∑ a ∈ Finset.univ.filter (fun a => f a = b), M.effect a
    70	  pos b := Finset.sum_nonneg fun a _ => M.pos a
    71	  sum_le_one := by
    72	    calc
    73	      ∑ b, ∑ a ∈ Finset.univ.filter (fun a => f a = b), M.effect a
    74	          = ∑ a, M.effect a := Finset.sum_fiberwise Finset.univ f M.effect
    75	      _ ≤ 1 := M.sum_le_one
    76	
    77	/-- Restatement of `sum_le_one` in terms of the named total operator. -/
    78	theorem total_le_one (M : Submeasurement α d) :
    79	    M.total ≤ 1 := by
    80	  simpa [total] using M.sum_le_one
    81	
    82	/-- Postprocessing preserves the sum of all effects. -/
    83	theorem postprocess_sum_eq [DecidableEq α] [DecidableEq β]
    84	    (M : Submeasurement α d) (f : α → β) :
    85	    ∑ a, M.effect a = ∑ b, (M.postprocess f).effect b :=
    86	  (Finset.sum_fiberwise Finset.univ f M.effect).symm
    87	
    88	/-- Postprocessing preserves the named total operator. -/
    89	theorem postprocess_total [DecidableEq α] [DecidableEq β]
    90	    (M : Submeasurement α d) (f : α → β) :
    91	    (M.postprocess f).total = M.total := by
    92	  simpa [total] using (M.postprocess_sum_eq f).symm
    93	
    94	end Submeasurement
    95	
    96	namespace Measurement
    97	
    98	variable {d : Type*} [Fintype d] [DecidableEq d]
    99	variable {α β : Type*} [Fintype α] [Fintype β]
   100	
   101	/--
   102	Build a complete measurement from effects whose sum is exactly the identity.
   103	
   104	This constructor keeps the equality proof as the primary hypothesis and derives
   105	the inherited submeasurement inequality automatically.  It is useful at paper
   106	sites that are explicitly POVMs rather than relaxed sub-POVMs.
   107	-/
   108	def ofSumEqOne (effect : α → Op d) (pos : ∀ a, 0 ≤ effect a)
   109	    (sum_eq_one : ∑ a, effect a = 1) : Measurement α d where
   110	  effect := effect
   111	  pos := pos
   112	  sum_le_one := le_of_eq sum_eq_one
   113	  sum_eq_one := sum_eq_one
   114	
   115	/-- The named total of a complete measurement is the identity. -/
   116	theorem total_eq_one (M : Measurement α d) :
   117	    M.total = 1 :=
   118	  M.sum_eq_one
   119	
   120	/--
   121	Postprocess a complete measurement by relabeling outcomes.
   122	
   123	This formalizes `references/ldt-paper/preliminaries.tex:169--180`: regrouping
   124	the effects along the fibers of `f` preserves the total operator, so a POVM
   125	remains a POVM after postprocessing.
   126	-/
   127	noncomputable def postprocess [DecidableEq α] [DecidableEq β]
   128	    (M : Measurement α d) (f : α → β) : Measurement β d where
   129	  toSubmeasurement := M.toSubmeasurement.postprocess f
   130	  sum_eq_one := by
   131	    calc
   132	      ∑ b, ∑ a ∈ Finset.univ.filter (fun a => f a = b), M.effect a
   133	          = ∑ a, M.effect a := Finset.sum_fiberwise Finset.univ f M.effect
   134	      _ = 1 := M.sum_eq_one
   135	
   136	@[simp] theorem postprocess_effect [DecidableEq α] [DecidableEq β]
   137	    (M : Measurement α d) (f : α → β) (b : β) :
   138	    (M.postprocess f).effect b =
   139	      ∑ a ∈ Finset.univ.filter (fun a => f a = b), M.effect a :=
   140	  rfl
   141	
   142	@[simp] theorem postprocess_to_submeasurement [DecidableEq α] [DecidableEq β]
   143	    (M : Measurement α d) (f : α → β) :
   144	    (M.postprocess f).toSubmeasurement = M.toSubmeasurement.postprocess f :=
   145	  rfl
   146	
   147	/-- A complete measurement is determined by its effects. -/
   148	theorem ext {M N : Measurement α d} (h : ∀ a, M.effect a = N.effect a) :
   149	    M = N := by
   150	  cases M with
   151	  | mk M hM =>
   152	      cases N with
   153	      | mk N hN =>
   154	          cases M with
   155	          | mk effectM posM leM =>
   156	              cases N with
   157	              | mk effectN posN leN =>
   158	                  simp only at h
   159	                  have heffect : effectM = effectN := funext h
   160	                  subst effectN
   161	                  rfl
   162	
   163	/-- Relabeling along `f` and then along `g` is relabeling along `g ∘ f`: the
   164	fiber of `g ∘ f` over `c` is the disjoint union of the fibers of `f` over the
   165	fiber of `g` over `c`, and regrouping a finite sum of effects along it does not
   166	change the sum. -/
   167	theorem postprocess_comp {γ : Type*} [Fintype γ]
   168	    [DecidableEq α] [DecidableEq β] [DecidableEq γ]
   169	    (M : Measurement α d) (f : α → β) (g : β → γ) :
   170	    (M.postprocess f).postprocess g = M.postprocess (fun a => g (f a)) := by
   171	  classical
   172	  apply ext
   173	  intro c
   174	  calc
   175	    ((M.postprocess f).postprocess g).effect c =
   176	        ∑ b : β, if g b = c then
   177	          ∑ a : α, if f a = b then M.effect a else 0
   178	        else 0 := by
   179	          change (∑ b ∈ Finset.univ.filter (fun b : β => g b = c),
   180	            ∑ a ∈ Finset.univ.filter (fun a : α => f a = b), M.effect a) = _
   181	          rw [Finset.sum_filter]
   182	          apply Finset.sum_congr rfl
   183	          intro b _
   184	          by_cases hgb : g b = c
   185	          · simp only [hgb, if_true]
   186	            rw [Finset.sum_filter]
   187	          · simp [hgb]
   188	    _ = ∑ b : β, ∑ a : α,
   189	        if g b = c ∧ f a = b then M.effect a else 0 := by
   190	          apply Finset.sum_congr rfl
   191	          intro b _
   192	          by_cases hgc : g b = c <;> simp [hgc]
   193	    _ = ∑ a : α, ∑ b : β,
   194	        if g b = c ∧ f a = b then M.effect a else 0 := by
   195	          rw [Finset.sum_comm]
   196	    _ = ∑ a : α,
   197	        if g (f a) = c then M.effect a else 0 := by
   198	          apply Finset.sum_congr rfl
   199	          intro a _
   200	          by_cases hgc : g (f a) = c
   201	          · rw [Finset.sum_eq_single (f a)]
   202	            · simp [hgc]
   203	            · intro b _ hba
   204	              by_cases hfa : f a = b
   205	              · exact (hba hfa.symm).elim
   206	              · simp [hfa]
   207	            · simp
   208	          · have hzero :
   209	                (∑ b : β,
   210	                  if g b = c ∧ f a = b then M.effect a else 0) = 0 := by
   211	              apply Finset.sum_eq_zero
   212	              intro b _
   213	              by_cases hfa : f a = b
   214	              · subst b
   215	                simp [hgc]
   216	              · simp [hfa]
   217	            simp [hgc, hzero]
   218	    _ = (M.postprocess (fun a => g (f a))).effect c := by
   219	          change _ = ∑ a ∈ Finset.univ.filter
   220	            (fun a : α => g (f a) = c), M.effect a
   221	          rw [Finset.sum_filter]
   222	
   223	end Measurement
   224	
   225	/-! ## Overlap definitions -/
   226	
   227	section Overlap
   228	
   229	variable {d : Type*} [Fintype d] [DecidableEq d]
   230	variable {α : Type*} [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α]
   231	
   232	/-- The off-diagonal overlap mass `∑_{a ≠ b} τ(M_a N_b)`. -/
   233	noncomputable def inconsistency (M N : α → Op d) : ℂ :=
   234	  ∑ a, ∑ b ∈ Finset.univ.filter (fun b => b ≠ a), normalizedTrace (M a * N b)
   235	
   236	/-- The diagonal overlap mass `∑_a τ(M_a N_a)`. -/
   237	noncomputable def diagOverlap (M N : α → Op d) : ℂ :=
   238	  ∑ a, normalizedTrace (M a * N a)
   239	
   240	end Overlap
   241	
   242	end MIPStarRE.Quantum

     3	/-!
     4	# Low-degree consistency transport
     5	
     6	This module identifies the low individual degree polynomial outcomes with the
     7	bounded polynomial representatives used by the directly indexed QPBT game.  It
     8	also transports complete measurements and their evaluation postprocessings
     9	without changing either coordinate order or consistency error.
    10	
    11	## References
    12	
    13	- `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:393-458`
    14	- `references/ldt-paper/test_definition.tex:180-202`
    15	- `docs/paper-gaps/qpbt_ld-dimension-divisibility.tex`
    16	-/
    17	
    18	open scoped BigOperators Matrix MatrixOrder ComplexOrder
    19	
    20	namespace MIPStarRE.QPBT
    21	
    22	open MIPStarRE.LDT
    23	open MIPStarRE.LDT.Preliminaries
    24	open MIPStarRE.Quantum
    25	
    26	noncomputable section
    27	
    28	/-! ## Polynomial outcomes -/
    29	
    30	private theorem directPolynomialRename_degreeOf_le
    31	    (D : DirectLdParams) (p : MvPolynomial (Fin D.m) (DirectScalarQ D))
    32	    (hp : ∀ i, MvPolynomial.degreeOf i p ≤ D.d) (i : Fin D.m) :
    33	    MvPolynomial.degreeOf i (MvPolynomial.rename Fin.rev p) ≤ D.d := by
    34	  rw [← Fin.rev_rev i,
    35	    MvPolynomial.degreeOf_rename_of_injective Fin.rev_injective]
    36	  exact hp (Fin.rev i)
    37	
    38	private theorem ldtPolynomial_ext
    39	    {params : Parameters} [FieldModel params.q]
    40	    {g h : MIPStarRE.LDT.Polynomial params} (hpoly : g.poly = h.poly) : g = h := by
    41	  cases g with
    42	  | mk gp hg =>
    43	      cases h with
    44	      | mk hp hh =>
    45	          simp only at hpoly
    46	          subst hp
    47	          rfl
    48	
    49	/-- Bounded QPBT polynomial representatives are equivalent to LDT
    50	polynomial outcomes.  The variable renaming is the same coordinate reversal
    51	as `directPointEquiv`, so evaluation retains the direct coordinate order. -/
    52	noncomputable def directPolyEquivPolynomial (D : DirectLdParams) :
    53	    letI := D.toLDTFieldModel
    54	    PolyIndex D.m (DirectScalarQ D) D.d ≃
    55	      MIPStarRE.LDT.Polynomial D.toLDTParameters := by
    56	  letI := D.toLDTFieldModel
    57	  refine
    58	    { toFun := fun g =>
    59	        { poly := MvPolynomial.rename Fin.rev g.1
    60	          lowIndividualDegree := directPolynomialRename_degreeOf_le D g.1
    61	            (degreeOf_le_of_mem_polyFunc g.2) }
    62	      invFun := fun g =>
    63	        ⟨MvPolynomial.rename Fin.rev g.poly, ?_⟩
    64	      left_inv := ?_
    65	      right_inv := ?_ }
    66	  · rw [MvPolynomial.mem_restrictDegree]
    67	    intro s hs i
    68	    exact (MvPolynomial.degreeOf_le_iff.mp
    69	      (directPolynomialRename_degreeOf_le D g.poly g.lowIndividualDegree i)) s hs
    70	  · intro g
    71	    apply Subtype.ext
    72	    change MvPolynomial.rename Fin.rev
    73	      (MvPolynomial.rename Fin.rev g.1) = g.1
    74	    rw [MvPolynomial.rename_rename]
    75	    rw [show Fin.rev ∘ Fin.rev = id by funext i; simp]
    76	    exact MvPolynomial.rename_id_apply g.1
    77	  · intro g
    78	    cases g with
    79	    | mk p hp =>
    80	        have hpoly : MvPolynomial.rename Fin.rev
    81	            (MvPolynomial.rename Fin.rev p) = p := by
    82	          rw [MvPolynomial.rename_rename]
    83	          rw [show Fin.rev ∘ Fin.rev = id by funext i; simp]
    84	          exact MvPolynomial.rename_id_apply p
    85	        apply ldtPolynomial_ext
    86	        exact hpoly
    87	
    88	@[simp] theorem directPolyEquivPolynomial_poly
    89	    (D : DirectLdParams) (g : PolyIndex D.m (DirectScalarQ D) D.d) :
    90	    letI := D.toLDTFieldModel
    91	    (directPolyEquivPolynomial D g).poly = MvPolynomial.rename Fin.rev g.1 := by
    92	  letI := D.toLDTFieldModel
    93	  rfl
    94	
    95	/-- The polynomial equivalence commutes with evaluation after the direct point
    96	and scalar codings. -/
    97	@[simp] theorem directPolyEquivPolynomial_apply
    98	    (D : DirectLdParams) (g : PolyIndex D.m (DirectScalarQ D) D.d)
    99	    (u : Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D) :
   100	    letI := D.toLDTFieldModel
   101	    directPolyEquivPolynomial D g (directPointEquiv D u) =
   102	      directScalarEquiv D (MvPolynomial.eval u g.1) := by
   103	  letI := D.toLDTFieldModel
   104	  unfold MIPStarRE.LDT.Polynomial.toFun evalPolynomialModel
   105	  rw [directPolyEquivPolynomial_poly]
   106	  unfold decodePoint
   107	  rw [MvPolynomial.eval_rename]
   108	  congr 1
   109	  apply congrArg (fun v : Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D =>
   110	    MvPolynomial.eval v g.1)
   111	  funext i
   112	  simp only [Function.comp_apply, directPointEquiv_apply, Fin.rev_rev]
   113	  change (directScalarEquiv D).symm (directScalarEquiv D (u i)) = u i
   114	  exact (directScalarEquiv D).symm_apply_apply (u i)
   115	
   116	/-! ## Complete measurements -/
   117	
   118	/-- Regard a complete LDT measurement as a matrix-valued QPBT
   119	measurement, with exactly the same effects. -/
   120	noncomputable def ldtMeasurementToMatrixMeasurement
   121	    {alpha iota : Type*} [Fintype alpha] [Fintype iota] [DecidableEq iota]
   122	    (M : MIPStarRE.LDT.Measurement alpha iota) :
   123	    MIPStarRE.Quantum.Measurement alpha iota :=
   124	  MIPStarRE.Quantum.Measurement.ofSumEqOne M.outcome M.outcome_pos (by
   125	    rw [M.sum_eq_total, M.total_eq_one])
   126	
   127	@[simp] theorem ldtMeasurementToMatrixMeasurement_effect
   128	    {alpha iota : Type*} [Fintype alpha] [Fintype iota] [DecidableEq iota]
   129	    (M : MIPStarRE.LDT.Measurement alpha iota) (a : alpha) :
   130	    (ldtMeasurementToMatrixMeasurement M).effect a = M.outcome a :=
   131	  rfl
   132	
   133	/-- Relabel an LDT polynomial projective measurement by direct QPBT
   134	polynomial representatives. -/
   135	noncomputable def directPolynomialMeasurement
   136	    (D : DirectLdParams) :
   137	    letI := D.toLDTFieldModel
   138	    {iota : Type*} → [Fintype iota] → [DecidableEq iota] →
   139	      ProjMeas (MIPStarRE.LDT.Polynomial D.toLDTParameters) iota →
   140	        PolyMeas D.m (DirectScalarQ D) D.d iota := by
   141	  letI := D.toLDTFieldModel
   142	  intro iota _ _ G
   143	  exact matrixMeasurementTransport (directPolyEquivPolynomial D).symm
   144	    (ldtMeasurementToMatrixMeasurement G.toMeasurement)
   145	
   146	@[simp] theorem directPolynomialMeasurement_effect
   147	    (D : DirectLdParams) :
   148	    letI := D.toLDTFieldModel
   149	    ∀ {iota : Type*} [Fintype iota] [DecidableEq iota]
   150	      (G : ProjMeas (MIPStarRE.LDT.Polynomial D.toLDTParameters) iota)
   151	      (g : PolyIndex D.m (DirectScalarQ D) D.d),
   152	      (directPolynomialMeasurement D G).effect g =
   153	        G.outcome (directPolyEquivPolynomial D g) := by
   154	  letI := D.toLDTFieldModel
   155	  intro iota _ _ G g
   156	  rfl
   157	
   158	/-- Extract one polynomial coordinate from a direct polynomial-tuple POVM. -/
   159	noncomputable def directPolyMeasTupleMarginal
   160	    (D : DirectLdParams) {iota : Type*} [Fintype iota] [DecidableEq iota]
   161	    (G : DirectPolyMeasTuple D iota) (r : Fin D.k) :
   162	    PolyMeas D.m (DirectScalarQ D) D.d iota :=
   163	  G.postprocess (fun tuple => tuple r)
   164	
   165	/-- Extract one polynomial coordinate from a seed-indexed polynomial-tuple
   166	POVM. -/
   167	noncomputable def polyMeasTupleMarginal
   168	    (L : LdParams) {iota : Type*} [Fintype iota] [DecidableEq iota]
   169	    (G : PolyMeasTuple L iota) (r : Fin L.k) :
   170	    PolyMeas L.m (ScalarQ L) L.d iota :=
   171	  G.postprocess (fun tuple => tuple r)
   172	
   173	/-- Evaluating a direct polynomial tuple and then selecting coordinate `r`
   174	agrees with evaluating the `r`-th polynomial marginal. -/
   175	theorem directPolyMeasTuple_evaluation_marginal
   176	    (D : DirectLdParams) {iota : Type*} [Fintype iota] [DecidableEq iota]
   177	    (G : DirectPolyMeasTuple D iota) (r : Fin D.k)
   178	    (u : Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D) :
   179	    (G.postprocess (evalDirectPolyTupleAt u)).postprocess (fun values => values r) =
   180	      (directPolyMeasTupleMarginal D G r).postprocess

    16	private lemma rolePairCond_mul {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    17	    (rL₁ rR₁ rL₂ rR₂ : Role) (X Y : MIPStarRE.Quantum.Op (ι × ι)) :
    18	    rolePairCond rL₁ rR₁ X * rolePairCond rL₂ rR₂ Y =
    19	      Matrix.reindex (roleRegisterPairLocalEquiv ι) (roleRegisterPairLocalEquiv ι)
    20	        (opTensor (rolePairProj rL₁ rR₁ * rolePairProj rL₂ rR₂) (X * Y)) := by
    21	  calc
    22	    rolePairCond rL₁ rR₁ X * rolePairCond rL₂ rR₂ Y
    23	      = Matrix.reindex (roleRegisterPairLocalEquiv ι) (roleRegisterPairLocalEquiv ι)
    24	          ((opTensor (rolePairProj rL₁ rR₁) X) *
    25	            (opTensor (rolePairProj rL₂ rR₂) Y)) := by
    26	              exact
    27	                (map_mul (Matrix.reindexAlgEquiv ℂ ℂ (roleRegisterPairLocalEquiv ι))
    28	                  (opTensor (rolePairProj rL₁ rR₁) X)
    29	                  (opTensor (rolePairProj rL₂ rR₂) Y)).symm
    30	    _ = Matrix.reindex (roleRegisterPairLocalEquiv ι) (roleRegisterPairLocalEquiv ι)
    31	          (opTensor (rolePairProj rL₁ rR₁ * rolePairProj rL₂ rR₂) (X * Y)) := by
    32	            rw [opTensor_mul]

    34	private lemma rolePairCond_mul_same {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]

    36	    rolePairCond rL rR X * rolePairCond rL rR Y = rolePairCond rL rR (X * Y) := by
    37	  have hproj : rolePairProj rL rR * rolePairProj rL rR = rolePairProj rL rR := by
    38	    simp [rolePairProj, opTensor_mul, roleProj_mul_self]
    39	  simpa [rolePairCond, hproj] using
    40	    rolePairCond_mul rL rR rL rR X Y

    42	private lemma rolePairCond_mul_eq_zero_of_ne {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    43	    (rL₁ rR₁ rL₂ rR₂ : Role) (X Y : MIPStarRE.Quantum.Op (ι × ι))
    44	    (h : (rL₁, rR₁) ≠ (rL₂, rR₂)) :
    45	    rolePairCond rL₁ rR₁ X * rolePairCond rL₂ rR₂ Y = 0 := by

    49	private lemma opTensor_roleCond {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]

    52	      rolePairCond rL rR (opTensor X Y) := by
    53	  ext x y
    54	  rcases x with ⟨⟨sL, iL⟩, ⟨sR, iR⟩⟩
    55	  rcases y with ⟨⟨tL, jL⟩, ⟨tR, jR⟩⟩
    56	  cases rL <;> cases rR <;> cases sL <;> cases sR <;> cases tL <;> cases tR <;>

   241	/-!
   242	The diagonal-block conditional expectation preserves either mixed defect
   243	exactly because the point measurement on the opposite carrier is constant on
   244	the residue register.  It does not yield a global/global compression theorem:
   245	the lifted state pairs equal residues, whereas separately compressing both
   246	polynomial measurements produces an independent double average over residues.
   247	Neither quantity bounds the other in general.  This open obstruction is
   248	recorded in `docs/paper-gaps/qpbt_ld-dimension-divisibility.tex`.

   251	/-- The normalized diagonal-block average of an operator on a carrier with a
   252	finite ancillary register.  This is the local conditional expectation used to
   253	discard one half of the correlated seed-residue ancilla. -/
   254	noncomputable def averageDiagonalBlock
   255	    {iota block : Type*} [Fintype iota] [Fintype block]
   256	    (A : Op (iota × block)) : Op iota := by
   257	  classical
   258	  exact (Fintype.card block : ℝ)⁻¹ •
   259	    ∑ r, A.submatrix (fun i => (i, r)) (fun i => (i, r))
   260	
   261	/-- Compress a POVM through the normalized diagonal-block average.  The
   262	nonemptiness assumption says precisely that the normalized finite average is
   263	defined over at least one ancillary basis element. -/
   264	noncomputable def correlatedAncillaCompressMeasurement
   265	    {alpha iota block : Type*}
   266	    [Fintype alpha] [Fintype iota] [DecidableEq iota]
   267	    [Fintype block] [DecidableEq block] [Nonempty block]
   268	    (M : MIPStarRE.Quantum.Measurement alpha (iota × block)) :
   269	    MIPStarRE.Quantum.Measurement alpha iota :=
   270	  MIPStarRE.Quantum.Measurement.ofSumEqOne
   271	    (fun a => averageDiagonalBlock (M.effect a))
   272	    (fun a => by
   273	      unfold averageDiagonalBlock
   274	      apply smul_nonneg
   275	      · positivity
   276	      · exact Finset.sum_nonneg fun r _ =>
   277	          Matrix.nonneg_iff_posSemidef.mpr
   278	            ((Matrix.nonneg_iff_posSemidef.mp (M.pos a)).submatrix
   279	              (fun i => (i, r))))
   280	    (by
   281	      classical
   282	      ext i j
   283	      simp only [averageDiagonalBlock, Matrix.sum_apply, Matrix.smul_apply,
   284	        Matrix.submatrix_apply]
   285	      calc
   286	        ∑ a, (Fintype.card block : ℝ)⁻¹ •
   287	              ∑ r, M.effect a (i, r) (j, r) =
   288	            (Fintype.card block : ℝ)⁻¹ •
   289	              ∑ a, ∑ r, M.effect a (i, r) (j, r) := by
   290	                rw [Finset.smul_sum]
   291	        _ = (Fintype.card block : ℝ)⁻¹ •
   292	              ∑ r, ∑ a, M.effect a (i, r) (j, r) := by
   293	                rw [Finset.sum_comm]
   294	        _ = (Fintype.card block : ℝ)⁻¹ •
   295	              ∑ r, (1 : Op (iota × block)) (i, r) (j, r) := by
   296	                congr 1
   297	                apply Finset.sum_congr rfl
   298	                intro r _
   299	                simpa only [Matrix.sum_apply] using
   300	                  congrFun (congrFun M.sum_eq_one (i, r)) (j, r)
   301	        _ = (1 : Op iota) i j := by
   302	              simp [Matrix.one_apply, Fintype.card_ne_zero])

   394	We define a special class of measurements that are relevant to the soundness
   395	properties of the low-degree test.

   397	\begin{definition}[Low-degree polynomial measurements]
   398	  \label{def:ld-meas}
   399	  Define $\polymeas{m}{d}{q}$ to be the set of POVM measurements whose outcomes
   400	  correspond to (individual) degree-$d$ polynomials of $m$ variables over
   401	  $\F_q$.
   402	  More generally, for an integer $\ldc$ and tuples $m=(m_1, m_2, \ldots,
   403	  m_\ldc)$, $d=(d_1, d_2, \ldots, d_\ldc)$ and $q=(q_1, q_2, \ldots, q_\ldc)$,
   404	  we let $\simulpolymeas{m}{d}{q}{\ldc}$ be the set of measurements $G =
   405	  \{G_{g_1,\, g_2,\, \ldots\,,\, g_\ldc}\}$ such that for $i\in\{1, 2, \ldots,
   406	  \ldc\}$, $g_i$ is a polynomial $g_i:\F_{q_i}^{m_i} \rightarrow
   407	  \F_{q_i}$ with individual degree $d_i$ (see \Cref{sec:ld-encoding} for a definition of individual degree). 
   408	\end{definition}
   409	
   410	Quantum soundness of a version of the classical low-degree test for polynomials of low \emph{total} degree was claimed
   411	in~\cite{natarajan2018low}, building on an analysis of a three-prover version of the test in~\cite{vidick2016three}. Unfortunately there is a gap in the soundness analysis of this test. For our construction we use the low individual degree test, whose quantum soundness is shown in~\cite{ML20} and generalized in~\cite{ji2021quantum}. We state the result in the form that is most directly useful for us, and show how the stated result follows from~\cite{ji2021quantum}.
   412	
   413	\begin{theorem}[Quantum soundness of the simultaneous classical low-degree test]
   414	  \label{lem:ld-soundness}
   415	  There exists a function $\delta_{\ld}(\eps, q, m, d, \ldc) = a (dm \ldc)^a (\eps^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bmd})$ for universal constants $a\geq 1$ and $0<b\leq 1$ 
   416	such that the following
   417	  holds.
   418	  For all $\eps > 0$ and parameter tuple $\ldparams = (q, m, d, \ldc)$, for all
   419	  projective strategies $(\psi,A,B)$ that succeed with probability at least
   420	  $1-\eps$ in the game $\game^\ld_\ldparams$, there exists measurements
   421	  \[G^w \in \simulpolymeas{m}{d}{q}{\ldc}\] on $\mH_w$, for
   422	  $w\in\{\alice,\bob\}$, such that
   423	  \begin{equation*}
   424	    \begin{split}
   425	      A^{\Point,\, u}_{a_1,\, a_2,\, \ldots\,,\, a_\ldc}
   426	      & \abc[\delta_{\ld}]
   427	      G^\bob_{[(g_1(u),g_2(u),\ldots,g_\ldc(u)) = (a_1,\, a_2,\, \ldots \,,\, a_\ldc)]}\;,\\
   428	      G^\alice_{[(g_1(u),g_2(u),\ldots,g_\ldc(u)) = (a_1,\, a_2,\, \ldots \,,\, a_\ldc)]}
   429	      & \abc[\delta_{\ld}]
   430				 B^{\Point,\, u}_{a_1,\, a_2,\, \ldots\,,\, a_\ldc}\;,\\
   431	      G^\alice_{g_1,\, g_2,\, \ldots \,,\, g_\ldc}
   432	      & \abc[\delta_{\ld}]
   433	      G^\bob_{g_1,\, g_2,\, \ldots \,,\, g_\ldc}\;,
   434	    \end{split}
   435	  \end{equation*}

    60	
    61	Throughout, $q = 2^k$ with $k$ odd is an admissible field size, the tuple
    62	$(q,m,d)$ is admissible when moreover $d \ge 1$ and $m \mid q$, and
    63	$\mathrm{ideg}_{d,m}(\F_q)$ denotes the $m$-variate polynomial representatives
    64	over $\F_q$ of individual degree at most $d$.  The comparison involves four
    65	theorem forms.
    66	\begin{enumerate}
    67	  \item \textbf{Source theorem form} (the polynomial-pair measurement).  There
    68	  is a function $\delta_S(\eps,m,d,q) = a(md)^a(\eps^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bmd})$,
    69	  for universal constants $a > 1$ and $0 < b < 1$, such that for every
    70	  admissible $(q,m,d)$ and every projective strategy for the Pauli basis test
    71	  succeeding with probability at least $1-\eps$, there is a projective
    72	  measurement $\{\hat S_{g_X,g_Z}\}$ with outcomes pairs of polynomials in
    73	  $\mathrm{ideg}_{d,m}(\F_q)$ whose evaluations are $\delta_S$-consistent, on
    74	  average over a uniform point $u \in \F_q^m$ and in both bases
    75	  $W \in \{X,Z\}$, with the corresponding points measurements
    76	  $\{\hat M^{(\mathrm{Point},W),u}_a\}$ of the strategy, together with the
    77	  symmetric counterpart of this relation.
    78	  \item \textbf{Missing instantiation obligation.}  The classical low
    79	  individual degree game with parameter tuple $(q,\, 2m+2,\, d,\, 1)$ is well
    80	  defined, and the combined point and line measurements assembled in the
    81	  analysis constitute a strategy for it of value at least
    82	  $1 - \delta_{\mathrm{combine}}$.  The game's question distribution draws
    83	  its axis and diagonal indices through an index function
    84	  $\chi_{2m+2}\colon \F_q \to \{1,\ldots,2m+2\}$ with classes of equal size
    85	  $q/(2m+2)$, so the game exists only when $2m+2$ divides $q$.
    86	  \item \textbf{Restricted form supported by the present route.}  The source
    87	  theorem form under the additional hypothesis $2m+2 \mid q$.  Among
    88	  admissible tuples this hypothesis holds exactly when $m = 1$ and
    89	  $q \ge 8$; it fails for every admissible tuple with $m \ge 2$ and for
    90	  $(q,m) = (2,1)$.

    92	  soundness of the directly indexed variant of the classical low individual

   108	\section{The source assertion and the obstruction}
   109	
   110	We examine the final step of the subsection ``Applying the classical
   111	low-degree test'' in the analysis of the Pauli basis test in the compression
   112	paper of Ji, Natarajan, Vidick, Wright, and Yuen (MIP$^{*}$=RE,
   113	arXiv:2001.04383), whose quantum soundness component builds on the low
   114	individual degree test of \cite{Ji2020LowIndividualDegree}.%
   115	\footnote{Tracked in \localissue{0002}.  In the mirror of the source
   116	consulted here, the polynomial-pair lemma and its proof are at
   117	\path{references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex},
   118	lines~1267--1288; the sub-line lemma is at lines~1063--1116 and the combined
   119	line lemma at lines~1020--1034 of the same file.  The game parametrization
   120	with its divisibility, the index function, the soundness statement with its
   121	proof, and admissibility are at
   122	\path{references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex},
   123	lines~33--35, 214--219, 413--458, and 958--961.}
   124	There, the combined point measurements
   125	$\{\hat Q^{x,z,\alpha,\beta}_c\}$ and combined line measurements
   126	$\{\hat Q^{\ell}_f\}$, indexed by points of $\F_q^{2m+2}$ and lines in
   127	$\F_q^{2m+2}$, are asserted to form a strategy for the classical low
   128	individual degree game with parameters
   129	\[
   130	  \mathsf{ldparams} = (q,\, 2m+2,\, d,\, 1)
   131	  \tag{\path{lem:qld-4-7}}
   132	\]
   133	of value $1 - \delta_{\mathrm{combine}}$, and the quantum soundness theorem
   134	for that game is applied to produce the global polynomial-pair measurement.
   135	The two lemmas feeding this step are stated for the line-point distribution
   136	over $\F_q^{2m+2}$.
   137	
   138	The game, however, is parametrized by tuples $(q,m',d,k)$ with $q$ an
   139	admissible field size \emph{and $m'$ dividing $q$}.  The divisibility is not
   140	incidental: the question distribution is a conditionally linear distribution
   141	in which a uniform seed coordinate $s \in \F_q$, read as an integer in
   142	$\{0,\ldots,q-1\}$, determines the axis or diagonal index through the unique
   143	$\chi(s)$ with
   144	\[
   145	  s = (\chi(s)-1)\,\frac{q}{m'} + r, \qquad 0 \le r < \frac{q}{m'},
   146	  \tag{\path{eq:chi-func}}
   147	\]
   148	so that the $m'$ classes $\chi^{-1}(i)$ partition $\F_q$ into sets of equal
   149	size $q/m'$ and the index is uniform.  For $m' \nmid q$ neither the index
   150	function nor the line-point distribution built from it is defined.
   151	
   152	Admissibility of $(q,m,d)$ supplies only $m \mid q$.  Since an admissible $q$
   153	is a power of two, $m \mid q$ forces $m = 2^j$.  For $j \ge 1$ the integer
   154	$m+1 \ge 3$ is odd, so $2m+2 = 2(m+1)$ has an odd factor exceeding $1$ and
   155	divides no power of two; for $m = 1$ the condition $4 \mid q$ holds for every
   156	admissible $q$ except $q = 2$.  Thus the instantiation at dimension $2m+2$ is
   157	undefined for every admissible tuple with $m \ge 2$: for instance
   158	$(q,m,d) = (8,2,1)$ is admissible, while $6 \nmid 8$.  The source performs
   159	the instantiation without addressing the divisibility, so its proof route
   160	establishes the polynomial-pair lemma, and with it the soundness theorem for
   161	the Pauli basis test that rests on it, only for $m = 1$ and $q \ge 8$.

   163	\section{What the cited soundness theorem requires: the import obligations}
   164	\label{sec:import-obligations}
   165	
   166	The quantum soundness theorem for the classical game inherits the constraint
   167	$m' \mid q$ solely because it is stated for the game just described; its
   168	proof fixes an admissible $q$ with $m' \mid q$, asserts that the game with
   169	simultaneity parameter $1$ is \emph{identical} to the two-prover tensor-code
   170	test for the Reed--Solomon tensor code $\mathcal C^{\ot m'}$ of the same
   171	authors' \emph{Quantum soundness of testing tensor codes} (arXiv:2111.08131)
   172	\cite{Ji2021Quantum}, and concludes by Theorem~4.7 there, instantiated with
   173	that theorem's auxiliary integer parameter --- denoted $k$ in that source,
   174	and written $K$ here to avoid clashing with the field exponent and the
   175	simultaneity parameter --- chosen as $(m')^3 d$.  Neither
   176	the asserted identity nor the instantiation is complete as stated, so the
   177	import carries two verification obligations, which this section details and
   178	which the blueprint's proof node for the soundness statement records as
   179	open.  Both obligations are independent of the divisibility question: they
   180	arise at every dimension, for the $\chi$-based game where it is defined and
   181	equally for the directly indexed variant proposed under the candidate
   182	repairs.
   183	
   184	\paragraph{The cited test.}
   185	In the two-prover tensor-code test (Figures~1 and~2 of
   186	\cite{Ji2021Quantum}; the two-prover strategy format and the goodness
   187	measure are Definitions~4.5 and~4.6 there), the referee performs one of
   188	three subtests with probability $1/3$ each, assigning the two roles of each
   189	subtest to the two provers uniformly at random.  \emph{Axis-parallel lines
   190	test}: sample a uniform point $u \in [n]^{m'}$ and a uniform axis
   191	$j \in \{1,\ldots,m'\}$; send the axis-parallel line $\ell$ through $u$ in
   192	direction $j$ to one prover, who answers a codeword $g \in \mathcal C$;
   193	send $u$ to the other, who answers a field value $a$; accept iff
   194	$g(u_j) = a$.  \emph{Subcube commutation test}: sample
   195	$j \in \{1,\ldots,m'\}$ and a subcube $H \subseteq [n]^{m'}$ by fixing the
   196	last $j-1$ coordinates uniformly; sample $u, v$ independently and uniformly
   197	in $H$ and a uniform order bit; send the ordered pair $(u,v)$ or $(v,u)$ to
   198	one prover, who answers a pair $(b_u, b_v)$ of field values; send $u$ to
   199	the other, who answers $a$; accept iff $b_u = a$.  \emph{Synchronicity
   200	test}: send one identical question --- a line, a point, or an ordered
   201	pair, with probability $1/3$ each --- to both provers and accept iff their
   202	answers agree.  Theorem~4.7 supposes a two-prover strategy passing this
   203	test with probability $1-\eps$ together with an integer parameter
   204	$K \ge 12 m' t$, where $t$ is the interpolation parameter of the base code
   205	--- for the degree-$d$ Reed--Solomon code, of blocklength $n = q$ and
   206	distance $q-d$, one has $t = d+1$ --- and produces projective measurements
   207	$\{G_c\}$ and $\{\tilde G_c\}$ with outcomes in $\mathcal C^{\ot m'}$,
   208	consistent with one prover's points measurements, with the other prover's
   209	lines measurements, and with each other, up to
   210	$\eta'(m',t,K,\eps,n^{-1}) = \mathrm{poly}(m',t,K) \cdot
   211	\mathrm{poly}(\eps, n^{-1}, e^{-K/(m')^2})$.
   212	
   213	\paragraph{Obligation 1: the game correspondence.}
   214	The source asserts that the $\chi$-based game at parameters $(q,m',d,1)$
   215	is this test.  It is not, in four respects.
   216	(i)~The game has no pair questions.  A pair question of the test reveals
   217	two points of a \emph{hidden} subcube --- the subcube itself is not sent
   218	--- and is answered by two field values, while the game's diagonal-line
   219	question reveals a full line description and is answered by a degree-$m'd$
   220	polynomial.  A reduction must construct the pair measurements from the
   221	diagonal-line measurements by post-processing (measure a line through $u$
   222	and $v$ and evaluate the answered polynomial at the two parameters), and
   223	both directions of the information mismatch matter: the game's line
   224	description carries an index and a seed, neither of which is a function of
   225	the pair $(u,v)$, so the constructed measurement must average over the
   226	compatible indices and seeds; and the game's diagonal lines fix the
   227	\emph{first} $i-1$ coordinates where the test's subcubes fix the
   228	\emph{last} $j-1$, so the coordinate conventions must be aligned.  The
   229	construction must preserve projectivity and must match the law of the
   230	hidden-subcube pair with the law induced by the game's diagonal sampling.
   231	(ii)~The game's line questions carry the seed $s \in \F_q$; the test's
   232	carry only the line.  A strategy may depend on the seed beyond its class
   233	$\chi^{-1}(i)$, and removing this dependence runs into the fiber-averaging
   234	difficulty made explicit under the candidate repairs: averaging preserves
   235	the line-versus-point branches exactly but not the synchronicity branches.
   236	(iii)~The branch weights differ: each nontrivial cross-test has mass $1/3$
   237	in the test against $2/9$ in the game.  Once the per-branch predicates are
   238	matched, the intended bookkeeping bound is that the constructed strategy's
   239	rejection probability in the test is at most $\tfrac32$ times the game's
   240	rejection probability, up to the $O(1/(m'q))$ of item~(iv); this bound is
   241	the target of the obligation, not an established fact.
   242	(iv)~The game's predicate fixes an acceptance convention on diagonal
   243	questions with zero direction --- an event of probability at most
   244	$2/(m'q)$, recorded in the blueprint's remark on zero directions --- for
   245	which the test has no counterpart branch.
   246	Finally, the displayed conclusions of Theorem~4.7 pair one prover's points
   247	measurements with the other prover's tensor-codeword measurement, and the
   248	first prover's tensor-codeword measurement with the second prover's lines
   249	measurements, while the game-level statement asserts the point consistency
   250	in both directions; deriving the stated form uses the role symmetrization
   251	of the test and belongs to the correspondence.  None of these steps is
   252	difficult to state, but none is carried out in the source, and together
   253	they replace the asserted one-line identity by a reduction carrying its
   254	own value bound.
   255	
   256	\paragraph{Obligation 2: the parameter bound.}
   257	Theorem~4.7 requires $K \ge 12 m' t = 12 m' (d+1)$.  The source
   258	instantiates $K = (m')^3 d$, which meets the bound iff
   259	$(m')^2 d \ge 12(d+1)$: this holds for all $d \ge 1$ when $m' \ge 5$,
   260	holds at $m' = 4$ exactly when $d \ge 3$, and fails for every $d$ when
   261	$m' \le 3$.  In the game's parameter domain the dimension divides the
   262	admissible field size and is therefore a power of two, so the source's
   263	instantiation violates the hypothesis exactly at $m' \in \{1,2\}$ for
   264	every $d$ and at $m' = 4$ for $d \in \{1,2\}$ --- in particular, in the
   265	multilinear regime $d = 1$, at every dimension $m' \le 4$.  A candidate
   266	repair is to instantiate $K = \max((m')^3 d,\, 12 m'(d+1))$; the open
   267	obligation is then to re-absorb the error, that is, to check that
   268	$\mathrm{poly}(m',t,K)$ and $e^{-K/(m')^2}$ still collapse to the form
   269	$a(dm')^a(\eps^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bm'd})$ in the small-$m'$ cases where the
   270	maximum is $12m'(d+1)$ --- plausible, since there
   271	$e^{-K/(m')^2} = e^{-12(d+1)/m'}$ decays in $d$ at a rate comparable to
   272	$2^{-m'd}$ for $m' \le 4$, but not checked here.
   273	
   274	In the correspondence of Obligation~1, the only role of the divisibility
   275	$m' \mid q$ is to make the $\chi$-sampled index uniform.  The underlying
   276	mathematics does not need the divisibility.  The low
   277	individual degree test of \cite{Ji2020LowIndividualDegree} samples its axis
   278	index $i$ uniformly from $\{1,\ldots,m'\}$ directly, with no index function
   279	on $\F_q$ and no divisibility hypothesis,%
   280	\footnote{See the test figure in \path{references/ldt-paper/test_definition.tex}.}
   281	and the tensor-code test is likewise a test about the code
   282	$\mathcal C^{\ot m'}$, not about an encoding of indices into $\F_q$.  The
   283	$\chi$-based packaging exists so that the question distribution is
   284	conditionally linear, which the introspection machinery requires for the
   285	game the players actually play --- the Pauli basis test at dimension $m$,
   286	where admissibility does supply the divisibility.  The game at dimension
   287	$2m+2$ never appears in a verifier; it is an internal analysis device in the
   288	proof of the polynomial-pair lemma, so nothing there requires its question
   289	distribution to be conditionally linear.
