   291	\section{Candidate repairs}
   292	
   293	\paragraph{Direct index sampling (candidate direction, recommended).}
   294	Define, for arbitrary $m' \ge 1$, the line-point distribution over
   295	$\F_q^{m'}$ that samples the uniform point, the uniform axis index
   296	$i \in \{1,\ldots,m'\}$, and the diagonal direction with vanishing first
   297	$i-1$ coordinates, directly; define the \emph{directly indexed game} with
   298	this question distribution, whose line questions carry the index $i$ (and,
   299	for diagonal lines, the projected direction) in place of the seed
   300	$s \in \F_q$; and state the imported soundness theorem for that game
   301	(form~4 above).  This removes the divisibility obstruction and nothing
   302	else: the directly indexed game still asks for polynomials on revealed
   303	lines, has no pair questions, and weighs its branches as the present game
   304	does, so establishing form~4 carries the same two import obligations as
   305	the $\chi$-based import (Section~\ref{sec:import-obligations}), now at
   306	arbitrary dimension.
   307	
   308	The relation to the present game when $m' \mid q$ must moreover be proved
   309	at the level of games, not merely of question distributions, because the
   310	two games have different question alphabets: an $\mathsf{ALine}$ question
   311	of the $\chi$-based game is a pair $(u_0, s)$ and a $\mathsf{DLine}$
   312	question a triple $(u_0, s, v')$, so a strategy may select different
   313	measurements for seeds $s \ne s'$ with $\chi(s) = \chi(s')$, and equality
   314	of the induced laws of the geometric data does not by itself transport
   315	such a strategy.  The transport layer decomposes into the following
   316	obligations, none of which is carried out here.
   317	\begin{itemize}
   318	  \item \emph{Distribution lemma.}  When $m' \mid q$, the image of the
   319	  conditionally linear question distribution under the parsing map
   320	  $(u_0,s) \mapsto (u_0,\chi(s))$, $(u_0,s,v') \mapsto (u_0,\chi(s),v')$
   321	  is the direct distribution, and conditioned on the parsed question the
   322	  seed is uniform on the class $\chi^{-1}(i)$, independently of everything
   323	  else.
   324	  \item \emph{Parsing pullback.}  A strategy for the directly indexed game
   325	  composed with the parsing map is a seed-oblivious strategy for the
   326	  $\chi$-based game.  Since the win predicate depends on the question only
   327	  through the parsed data, and a seed-oblivious strategy answers
   328	  identically across each fiber --- in particular on the synchronicity
   329	  branches, where both players hold the same seed --- the value should be
   330	  preserved exactly on every branch, and projectivity is preserved.  This
   331	  is the direction the combining subtree needs.
   332	  \item \emph{Seed-fiber averaging: what it preserves and what it does
   333	  not.}  In the opposite direction, average each line measurement over its
   334	  seed fiber: attach to a direct question $(u_0,i)$, respectively
   335	  $(u_0,i,v')$, the average over uniform $s \in \chi^{-1}(i)$ of the
   336	  measurements attached to $(u_0,s)$, respectively $(u_0,s,v')$, leaving
   337	  the points measurements unchanged.  By the conditional uniformity of the
   338	  seed this preserves the value of every \emph{line-versus-point} branch
   339	  exactly: there the paired question carries no seed, so the branch value
   340	  is an average over the fiber of per-seed values, which the averaged
   341	  measurement computes.  It does \emph{not} preserve the synchronicity
   342	  branches.  There both players hold the same seed, so the $\chi$-based
   343	  branch value is the diagonal average
   344	  $\E_{s}\sum_f \langle M^{(u_0,s)}_f \ot \widetilde M^{(u_0,s)}_f
   345	  \rangle$, while the averaged strategy realizes the double average
   346	  $\E_{s,s'}\sum_f \langle M^{(u_0,s)}_f \ot \widetilde M^{(u_0,s')}_f
   347	  \rangle$ over independent seeds in the fiber; the two differ whenever
   348	  the players' measurements vary across a fiber in a correlated way (if
   349	  both apply a common seed-dependent relabelling, every diagonal term is
   350	  large and the cross terms are not), and neither quantity dominates the
   351	  other in general.  An earlier revision of this note claimed that the
   352	  averaging preserves the exact value, and with it synchronicity; that
   353	  claim was wrong and is withdrawn.  What needs proof is control of the
   354	  synchronicity branches under de-seeding.  Candidate approaches: show
   355	  that a strategy of value $1-\eps$ in the $\chi$-based game is, with
   356	  polynomial loss, close to a seed-oblivious one; or state form~4 with a
   357	  synchronicity hypothesis in the doubled-average form and re-derive it on
   358	  the tensor-code side.  Choosing and proving one of these is an open
   359	  obligation.

    26	using a different mathematical route because an available formal-library theorem
    27	has a slightly different form.  Such a note is a mathematical note first, and a
    28	record of the formalization second: it should be readable by a mathematician or
    29	mathematical physicist who has not followed the issue discussion.
    30	
    31	The note should isolate the mathematical mechanism.  It should say what the
    32	cited source asserts, what the cited results actually imply, where a term or
    33	hypothesis is lost, and what statement the formal development proves instead.
    34	If the formal proof takes a different route, the note should explain the
    35	replacement argument and the hypotheses on which it rests.  This is especially
    36	important when the proof uses a theorem, construction, or convention from
    37	Mathlib which is not part of the cited argument.  In that case the note should
    38	state the Mathlib result in ordinary mathematical language, explain how it is
    39	specialized to the notation of the paper, and compare its hypotheses and
    40	conclusion with the step it replaces.  It should not merely say that \Lean{} did
    41	not accept a proof, that the modified proof compiles, or that a named library
    42	lemma was applied.
    43	
    44	The documents in this directory should themselves follow this standard.  A
    45	policy or template which reads like a checklist will tend to produce checklist
    46	notes; the examples and templates should therefore be written as mathematical
    47	prose.
    48	
    49	\section{Concision and Readability}
    50	
    51	A paper-gap note should be short enough that a reader can understand the issue
    52	in one sitting.  The first page should answer four questions: what the source
    53	uses, how hard the remaining formal work is, what the formalization or audit
    54	checked, and what the current verdict is.  Begin with a short
    55	\emph{At a glance} section when the note concerns an open or recently resolved
    56	formalization task.  That section should estimate the difficulty, the rough
    57	implementation weight, the split between Mathlib reuse and project-local work,
    58	and the key Mathlib APIs or modules.  Use honest ranges, not false precision.
    59	
    60	The \emph{Key theorem forms} section should be Section~2, immediately after
    61	\emph{At a glance}.  Put the theorem forms before the source details so the
    62	reader knows what the formalization is aiming to prove.  After that, keep the
    63	source assertion, the mechanism being checked, the blueprint/formal comparison,
    64	and the conclusion.  Use more sections only when a counterexample or long
    65	derivation genuinely needs room.
    66	
    67	Keep background to the minimum needed for the local point.  Prefer one clear
    68	special case over a general restatement of the surrounding theorem.  Use displayed
    69	equations for the source assertion, the key calculation, and the theorem forms;
    70	avoid displays for traceability data, declaration names, or long lists.  The
    71	blueprint/formal comparison should be compact and should not repeat the theorem
    72	forms.  The section ``Form of the Note'' below specifies where traceability data
    73	belongs; the body should read as mathematical prose, not as a log.
    74	
    75	If the verdict is that there is no mathematical discrepancy, say so plainly and
    76	stop.  Keep the conclusion highly compact, normally under twenty source lines.
    77	If the only remaining work is an implementation task, name it briefly and link
    78	the issue or pull request in a footnote.
    79	
    80	\section{When the Investigation Starts}
    81	
    82	The investigation starts when the obstruction appears to be mathematical rather
    83	than merely formal.  No final judgement is needed at this stage.  It is enough
    84	that, after reading the relevant source and attempting the corresponding formal
    85	statement, the proof seems to require a different scalar, an additional
    86	hypothesis, a different tensor placement, a distinction between two objects which
    87	the prose identifies, or an auxiliary assertion not supplied by the cited
    88	argument.
    89	
    90	The same investigation should also start when such a deviation is discovered
    91	after the fact.  If the existing formal development or informal blueprint has
    92	already changed the statement, strengthened a hypothesis, weakened a conclusion,
    93	inserted an unadvertised lemma, or replaced the cited proof by a different
    94	formal-library argument, the mathematical change should be documented even if all
    95	relevant files already compile.
    96	
    97	At this early stage the purpose is to preserve the question while it is still
    98	local.  The note may later conclude that the matter is only notational, that an
    99	intermediate estimate in the cited source needs a harmless correction, that a
   100	missing hypothesis is genuinely needed, or that no discrepancy remains.  Thus
   101	the trigger is not the severity of the eventual verdict, but the appearance of a
   102	real mismatch between the cited reasoning and the statement that can be
   103	formalized.
   104	
   105	A failed tactic search, a missing formal lemma, or an inconvenient coercion is
   106	not enough.  The obstruction must survive translation back into ordinary
   107	mathematics.
   108	
   109	Sometimes an investigation uncovers an improvement that is not a discrepancy:
   110	the formalization works correctly, but it could be simplified by using an
   111	existing library, replacing a custom type, or adopting a cleaner proof route.
   112	These are not, by themselves, paper-gap notes.  They are action items.  When
   113	such an improvement is identified, open a GitHub issue or pull request that
   114	describes the proposed change.  If the investigation also produces a paper-gap
   115	note, link the issue or pull request from that note: the note records the
   116	mathematical justification, and the issue or pull request drives the
   117	implementation.
   118	
   119	\section{When to Write a Note}
   120	
   121	A note should be written once the source argument and the formal proof no longer
   122	match as mathematical arguments.  This includes, for instance, a numerical
   123	estimate whose constant does not follow from the cited lemma, a displayed
   124	conclusion which uses an unstated hypothesis, or a step in which two objects are
   125	identified although they must remain distinct.  In analytic, algebraic,
   126	probabilistic, or quantum arguments, such distinctions may concern the domain of
   127	a map, the placement of a tensor factor, the type of an outcome, the distinction
   128	between a structure and a substructure, or the scalar carried by an approximation
   129	relation.
   130	
   131	A note is required when an audit finds that a Lean declaration associated with a
   132	source-labelled statement has acquired an extra non-source hypothesis, such as
   133	bridge, residual, repair, producer, or obligation-structure data.  Such a
   134	declaration is temporary proof debt, not a replacement for the source theorem,
   135	and should not be introduced merely to avoid a \verb|sorry|.  The note must say
   136	plainly that the Lean result is conditional, identify the source-faithful theorem
   137	form that remains to be proved, and give the intended obligation discharger or
   138	removal plan.  The blueprint should not mark the source-labelled statement with
   139	\verb|\leanok| by pointing to this conditional helper.
   140	
   141	Changing a Lean theorem away from the statement in
   142	\path{references/ldt-paper/} is strongly discouraged.  A paper-gap note should
   143	not make such a change look routine: it should explain the mathematical
   144	necessity, or else classify the change as proof debt to be removed.
   145	
   146	When an existing conditional helper is audited, the first task is to extract any
   147	argument it already contains into source-faithful lemmas.  If the remaining
   148	bridge hypothesis cannot be derived from the paper hypotheses, the formal
   149	development should restore the source theorem statement and record the missing
   150	proof obligation explicitly, rather than retaining the strengthened statement as
   151	though it were the paper theorem.
   152	
   153	This requirement is not meant to classify every explicit Lean side condition as
   154	a discrepancy.  Positivity, nonemptiness, decidability, field-model instances,
   155	and denominator nonvanishing hypotheses may be faithful encodings of the domain
   156	in which the paper's theorem is stated.  The note should distinguish such
   157	boundary hypotheses from hypotheses that supply an unproved step of the paper
   158	argument.
   159	
   160	A note is also appropriate when the proof becomes formal only after changing an
   161	intermediate scalar, weakening a conclusion, strengthening a hypothesis, or
   162	inserting an additional lemma which is not simply an expansion of the cited
   163	argument.  These are mathematical changes, even when they are harmless for the
   164	final theorem.  It is likewise appropriate when an available formal-library
   165	theorem proves the needed result under a somewhat different formulation from the
   166	cited source.  In that case the note should be deliberately pedagogical.  It
   167	should explain, in ordinary mathematical language, what the replacement result
   168	says, how it is specialized, which hypotheses are new or differently packaged,
   169	and why the resulting statement is a legitimate substitute for the step in the
   170	cited argument.  If the issue remains open after reasonable attempts, the note
   171	should say what has been checked and what remains unknown.
   172	
   173	\section{Counterexamples}
   174	
   175	If the cited assertion appears to be false, the note should not stop at saying
   176	that the proof cannot be formalized.  It should give the counterexample, or the
   177	smallest relevant part of it, in ordinary mathematical notation.  The example
   178	should be accompanied by enough verification that the reader can see both sides:
   179	the hypotheses of the cited assertion hold, and its conclusion fails.
   180	
   181	When feasible, the counterexample should also be formalized in \Lean{}.  This is
   182	especially valuable when the example is finite, algebraic, computational, or
   183	otherwise small enough that the failure can be checked without reproducing the
   184	whole surrounding theory.  The note should then state the mathematical content
   185	of the checked counterexample and identify the corresponding Lean declaration in
   186	a footnote.  The Lean file is not a substitute for the prose: the prose should
   187	still explain why the example refutes the cited assertion.
   188	
   189	\section{Revision of a Note}
   190	
   191	A paper-gap note may be provisional.  It may begin as soon as the mathematical
   192	obstruction has been isolated well enough to state the question, and it may be
   193	revised as the calculation, the blueprint, or the corresponding \Lean{}
   194	declarations become clearer.  The first version need not know the final
   195	classification, but it should say plainly which mathematical point is known and
   196	which point remains unsettled.
   197	
   198	Later revisions should not make the note into a chronological log.  They should
   199	rewrite the document so that it remains a coherent account of the present
   200	mathematical understanding.  If the verdict changes, the conclusion should state
   201	the current verdict; the linked issue or pull request can preserve the earlier
   202	discussion.
   203	
   204	\section{Form of the Note}
   205	
   206	Each note should stand on its own.  It should give the date, cite the relevant
   207	source article, and provide enough traceability for the reader to locate the
   208	original passage and the project discussion.  GitHub issues and pull requests may
   209	be linked with \verb|\href|, and source files, line ranges, and labels should be
   210	recorded when they help the reader check the claim.  These references should
   211	serve the exposition rather than govern it: the main text should be organized
   212	around the mathematical assertion and its proof.
   213	
   214	The note should introduce its notation before using it.  Symbols for
   215	measurements, tensor factors, approximation relations, and error parameters
   216	should be named in prose.  If an approximation relation is state-dependent, the
   217	state should be named, or its defining expression should be given when this can
   218	be done briefly.  Only after the notation is in place should the note state the
   219	assertion in the cited source, using a bibliographic citation such as
   220	\verb|\cite[Section~...]{...}| when the section or chapter is known.
   221	
   222	Only the relevant hypotheses should be reproduced.  If the question is a scalar
   223	substitution, a missing term, or a missing hypothesis, the note should not quote
   224	a long unrelated part of the proof.  It should give the cited lemma or
   225	proposition in the special case actually used, then display the calculation or
   226	logical implication in which the discrepancy appears.
   227	
   228	Displayed equations should be used with restraint.  They are appropriate for the
   229	source estimate being checked, the cited estimate in the form actually used, and
   230	the calculation where a term or hypothesis appears or disappears.  When a
   231	displayed equation is identified by a source label, the label should appear on
   232	the right of the display, while the surrounding prose refers to the mathematical
   233	assertion itself.  The standard \texttt{amsmath} command \verb|\tag| is the
   234	right mechanism for this; a separate local convention should be introduced only
   235	if the standard mechanism is genuinely insufficient.  For a multi-line aligned
   236	display, tag the individual lines that carry the source information rather than
   237	forcing a long combined label below the equations.  Short
   238	scalar definitions and elementary inequalities should remain inline when the
   239	sentence reads better that way.  As in ordinary mathematical writing, a displayed
   240	formula is part of the surrounding sentence and should be punctuated accordingly.
   241	
   242	Bibliographic entries used only by these notes should live in
   243	\path{docs/paper-gaps/references.bib}.  A new note should ordinarily begin from
   244	\path{docs/paper-gaps/template.tex}, which records the common LaTeX preamble,
   245	the local bibliography, and a model for right-hand source labels in displayed
   246	equations.
   247	
   248	Blueprint prose cites a note like any other source, with
   249	\verb|\cite{gap:<slug>}|; the bibliography entry in
   250	\path{blueprint/src/references.bib} carries the published URL of the note,
   251	whether the note lives in this repository or in another one.  Lean docstrings
   252	and comments use the repository path form \path{docs/paper-gaps/<slug>.tex}.
   253	
   254	The note should then compare the cited source with the informal blueprint, if
   255	there is one, and with the formal statement.  This comparison should be written
   256	in ordinary mathematical prose.  Formal declaration names and source paths should
   257	be supplied only to identify the exact formal statements, and normally belong in
   258	footnotes.
   259	
   260	The conclusion should give a verdict.  It may say that there is no discrepancy,

     LdQuestion P → LdQuestion P → LdAnswer P → LdAnswer P → Bool :=
   open Classical in

       if validLdAnswer tA a && validLdAnswer tB b then
         match tA, tB, a, b with
         | .point, .point, .pointVals u, .pointVals v => decide (u = v)
         | .aline, .point, .alinePolys f, .pointVals u =>

 \chapter{The Pauli basis test}
 \label{chap:qpbt-test}
 % Paper label sec:pauli-verifier kept for cross-reference fidelity; it resolves to this chapter.
 \label{sec:pauli-verifier}
 
 This chapter defines the two testing primitives underlying the question-reduction step: the \emph{classical low individual degree game}, in its simultaneous form, and the \emph{Pauli basis test}, a nonlocal game built from the classical game together with the Magic Square game. We state the quantum soundness of the classical game (Theorem~\ref{lem:ld-soundness}, imported, with the facts required by the identification, which remain to be proved, recorded in \cite{gap:qpbt_ld-dimension-divisibility}; see Remark~\ref{rem:ld-soundness-provider}), the rigidity of the Magic Square game (Theorem~\ref{thm:ms-rigidity}, imported), completeness of the Pauli basis test (Lemma~\ref{lem:pauli-completeness}), and the main soundness theorem for the Pauli basis test (Theorem~\ref{thm:pauli}), whose proof occupies Chapters~\ref{chap:qpbt-observables}--\ref{chap:qpbt-extraction} and is completed in Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-extraction} only modulo the proof obligation documented in \cite{gap:qpbt_ld-dimension-divisibility}. The chapter closes with the qubit form of the soundness statement (Corollary~\ref{cor:pauli-binary}) and the canonical parameter choice with its soundness bound (Definition~\ref{def:introparams}, Lemma~\ref{lem:delta-bound}).
 
 Throughout, the two players are denoted $\mathrm A$ and $\mathrm B$; for $w \in \{\mathrm A,\mathrm B\}$ we write $\overline w$ for the other player. Games, strategies, values, conditionally linear (CL) functions and distributions, typed distributions sampled from the edges of a graph, and the state-dependent approximation $\approx_\delta$ between families of measurement operators are as in Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-games}; the algebraic material on lines, canonical linear maps, the low-degree encoding, and generalized Pauli observables is from Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-algebra}.
 
 \section{The classical low individual degree game}
 % Paper labels sec:ld-verifier and sec:ld-game kept for cross-reference fidelity.
 \label{sec:ld-verifier}
 \label{sec:ld-game}
 
 The classical low individual degree game is a two-player game based on the low individual degree variant of the multilinearity test of Babai, Fortnow, and Lund. In the basic version, one player (the ``points player'') receives a uniformly random point $u \in \F_q^m$ and answers with a value $a \in \F_q$, while the other player (the ``lines player'') receives a random line through $u$ --- either axis-parallel or diagonal --- and answers with a univariate polynomial describing the restriction of a global function to that line. If the players share a polynomial $g\colon \F_q^m \to \F_q$ of individual degree at most $d$ and answer with $g(u)$ and with the restriction $g|_\ell$, they win with probability $1$; the soundness theorem below states that the converse approximately holds. In the simultaneous version, the players' answers are $k$-tuples, checked coordinatewise against a $k$-tuple of low individual degree polynomials.

 		L_{\mathsf{ALine}}(u,s,v) = \bigl(L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_{e_i}(u),\, s,\, 0\bigr)\quad\text{for all } (u,s,v) \in V\;,

 	(Definition~\ref{def:ld-question-distribution}) partitions $\F_q$ into
 	classes of equal size, one for each coordinate. The same divisibility
 	underlies the line-point distribution over $\F_q^{2m+2}$
 	(Definition~\ref{def:line-point-dist} instantiated at dimension
 	$2m+2$), and with it the statements of Lemmas~\ref{lem:qld-sublines}
 	and~\ref{lem:qld-4-13} and the proofs of all three of

 	and~\ref{lem:qld-4-7}. The condition that $2m+2$ divide $q$ does not
 	follow from admissibility of $(q,m,d)$
 	(Definition~\ref{def:admissible}), which supplies only that $m$
 	divides $q$; indeed the two are jointly satisfiable only in a
 	degenerate range. An admissible field size
 	(Definition~\ref{def:admissible-size}) is a power of two, so $m$
 	dividing $q$ forces $m$ to be a power of two; for $m \ge 2$ the
 	integer $m+1$ is odd and exceeds $1$, so $2m+2 = 2(m+1)$ divides no
 	power of two, while for $m = 1$ the condition $4 \mid q$ holds for
 	every admissible $q$ except $q = 2$. The source proof in
 	\cite{Ji2020MIPStar} performs the instantiation at dimension $2m+2$
 	without addressing the divisibility. The statements above are
 	therefore retained in their source form, and for admissible
 	parameters with $m \ge 2$ their proofs, like the source's, are
 	blocked at the marked steps, so the conclusions are not established

 	admissible parameter tuple requires a formulation of the game, of its
 	question distribution, and of Theorem~\ref{lem:ld-soundness} that
 	applies to dimensions not dividing $q$; the missing step and the
 	candidate repairs are analyzed in
 	\cite{gap:qpbt_ld-dimension-divisibility}.
 \end{remark}

   251	/-- The normalized diagonal-block average of an operator on a carrier with a
   252	finite ancillary register.  This is the local conditional expectation used to
   253	discard one half of the correlated seed-residue ancilla. -/
   254	noncomputable def averageDiagonalBlock
   255	    {iota block : Type*} [Fintype iota] [Fintype block]
   256	    (A : Op (iota × block)) : Op iota := by
   257	  classical
   258	  exact (Fintype.card block : ℝ)⁻¹ •
   259	    ∑ r, A.submatrix (fun i => (i, r)) (fun i => (i, r))
   260	
   261	/-- Compress a POVM through the normalized diagonal-block average.  The
   262	nonemptiness assumption says precisely that the normalized finite average is
   263	defined over at least one ancillary basis element. -/
   264	noncomputable def correlatedAncillaCompressMeasurement
   265	    {alpha iota block : Type*}
   266	    [Fintype alpha] [Fintype iota] [DecidableEq iota]
   267	    [Fintype block] [DecidableEq block] [Nonempty block]
   268	    (M : MIPStarRE.Quantum.Measurement alpha (iota × block)) :
   269	    MIPStarRE.Quantum.Measurement alpha iota :=
   270	  MIPStarRE.Quantum.Measurement.ofSumEqOne
   271	    (fun a => averageDiagonalBlock (M.effect a))
   272	    (fun a => by
   273	      unfold averageDiagonalBlock
   274	      apply smul_nonneg
   275	      · positivity
   276	      · exact Finset.sum_nonneg fun r _ =>
   277	          Matrix.nonneg_iff_posSemidef.mpr
   278	            ((Matrix.nonneg_iff_posSemidef.mp (M.pos a)).submatrix
   279	              (fun i => (i, r))))
   280	    (by
   281	      classical
   282	      ext i j
   283	      simp only [averageDiagonalBlock, Matrix.sum_apply, Matrix.smul_apply,
   284	        Matrix.submatrix_apply]
   285	      calc
   286	        ∑ a, (Fintype.card block : ℝ)⁻¹ •
   287	              ∑ r, M.effect a (i, r) (j, r) =
   288	            (Fintype.card block : ℝ)⁻¹ •
   289	              ∑ a, ∑ r, M.effect a (i, r) (j, r) := by
   290	                rw [Finset.smul_sum]
   291	        _ = (Fintype.card block : ℝ)⁻¹ •
   292	              ∑ r, ∑ a, M.effect a (i, r) (j, r) := by
   293	                rw [Finset.sum_comm]
   294	        _ = (Fintype.card block : ℝ)⁻¹ •
   295	              ∑ r, (1 : Op (iota × block)) (i, r) (j, r) := by
   296	                congr 1
   297	                apply Finset.sum_congr rfl
   298	                intro r _
   299	                simpa only [Matrix.sum_apply] using
   300	                  congrFun (congrFun M.sum_eq_one (i, r)) (j, r)
   301	        _ = (1 : Op iota) i j := by
   302	              simp [Matrix.one_apply, Fintype.card_ne_zero])
   303	
   304	@[simp] theorem correlatedAncillaCompressMeasurement_effect
   305	    {alpha iota block : Type*}
   306	    [Fintype alpha] [Fintype iota] [DecidableEq iota]
   307	    [Fintype block] [DecidableEq block] [Nonempty block]
   308	    (M : MIPStarRE.Quantum.Measurement alpha (iota × block)) (a : alpha) :
   309	    (correlatedAncillaCompressMeasurement M).effect a =
   310	      averageDiagonalBlock (M.effect a) :=
   311	  rfl
   312	
   313	private theorem averageDiagonalBlock_finset_sum
   314	    {alpha iota block : Type*} [Fintype iota] [Fintype block]
   315	    (s : Finset alpha) (A : alpha → Op (iota × block)) :
   316	    averageDiagonalBlock (∑ a ∈ s, A a) =
   317	      ∑ a ∈ s, averageDiagonalBlock (A a) := by
   318	  classical
   319	  ext i j
   320	  simp only [averageDiagonalBlock, Matrix.smul_apply, Matrix.sum_apply,
   321	    Matrix.submatrix_apply]
   322	  simp_rw [Finset.smul_sum]
   323	  rw [Finset.sum_comm]
   324	
   325	/-- Normalized diagonal-block compression commutes with deterministic outcome
   326	postprocessing. -/
   327	theorem correlatedAncillaCompressMeasurement_postprocess
   328	    {alpha beta iota block : Type*}
   329	    [Fintype alpha] [DecidableEq alpha]
   330	    [Fintype beta] [DecidableEq beta]
   331	    [Fintype iota] [DecidableEq iota]
   332	    [Fintype block] [DecidableEq block] [Nonempty block]
   333	    (M : MIPStarRE.Quantum.Measurement alpha (iota × block))
   334	    (f : alpha → beta) :
   335	    correlatedAncillaCompressMeasurement (M.postprocess f) =
   336	      (correlatedAncillaCompressMeasurement M).postprocess f := by
   337	  classical
   338	  apply MIPStarRE.Quantum.Measurement.ext
   339	  intro b
   340	  rw [MIPStarRE.Quantum.Measurement.postprocess_effect,
   341	    correlatedAncillaCompressMeasurement_effect,
   342	    MIPStarRE.Quantum.Measurement.postprocess_effect]
   343	  exact averageDiagonalBlock_finset_sum
   344	    (Finset.univ.filter (fun a => f a = b)) M.effect
   345	
   346	/-- Specialize ancillary compression to the nonempty residue fiber supplied by
   347	the divisibility data of `LdParams`. -/
   348	noncomputable def seedFiberCompressMeasurement
   349	    (L : LdParams) {alpha iota : Type*}
   350	    [Fintype alpha] [Fintype iota] [DecidableEq iota]
   351	    (M : MIPStarRE.Quantum.Measurement alpha
   352	      (iota × Fin (L.q / L.m))) :
   353	    MIPStarRE.Quantum.Measurement alpha iota := by
   354	  letI : Nonempty (Fin (L.q / L.m)) :=
   355	    Fin.pos_iff_nonempty.mp L.seedFiberCard_pos
   356	  exact correlatedAncillaCompressMeasurement M
   357	
   358	@[simp] theorem seedFiberCompressMeasurement_effect
   359	    (L : LdParams) {alpha iota : Type*}
   360	    [Fintype alpha] [Fintype iota] [DecidableEq iota]
   361	    (M : MIPStarRE.Quantum.Measurement alpha
   362	      (iota × Fin (L.q / L.m))) (a : alpha) :
   363	    (seedFiberCompressMeasurement L M).effect a =
   364	      averageDiagonalBlock (M.effect a) :=
   365	  rfl
   366	
   367	/-- Seed-fiber compression commutes with deterministic outcome
   368	postprocessing. -/
   369	theorem seedFiberCompressMeasurement_postprocess
   370	    (L : LdParams) {alpha beta iota : Type*}
   371	    [Fintype alpha] [DecidableEq alpha]
   372	    [Fintype beta] [DecidableEq beta]
   373	    [Fintype iota] [DecidableEq iota]
   374	    (M : MIPStarRE.Quantum.Measurement alpha
   375	      (iota × Fin (L.q / L.m))) (f : alpha → beta) :
   376	    seedFiberCompressMeasurement L (M.postprocess f) =
   377	      (seedFiberCompressMeasurement L M).postprocess f := by
   378	  letI : Nonempty (Fin (L.q / L.m)) :=
   379	    Fin.pos_iff_nonempty.mp L.seedFiberCard_pos
   380	  exact correlatedAncillaCompressMeasurement_postprocess M f
   381	
   382	/-- Compress a direct polynomial-tuple POVM from the correlated seed-residue
   383	carrier to the corresponding seed-indexed polynomial POVM. -/
   384	noncomputable def seedFiberCompressPolyMeasTuple
   385	    (L : LdParams) {iota : Type*} [Fintype iota] [DecidableEq iota]
   386	    (G : DirectPolyMeasTuple L.toDirectLdParams
   387	      (iota × Fin (L.q / L.m))) : PolyMeasTuple L iota := by
   388	  exact seedFiberCompressMeasurement L G
   389	
   390	@[simp] theorem seedFiberCompressPolyMeasTuple_effect
   391	    (L : LdParams) {iota : Type*} [Fintype iota] [DecidableEq iota]
   392	    (G : DirectPolyMeasTuple L.toDirectLdParams
   393	      (iota × Fin (L.q / L.m))) (g : PolyTuple L) :
   394	    (seedFiberCompressPolyMeasTuple L G).effect g =
   395	      averageDiagonalBlock (G.effect g) :=
   396	  rfl
   397	
   398	/-- Polynomial evaluation commutes exactly with compression of the correlated
   399	seed-residue carrier. -/
   400	theorem seedFiberCompressPolyMeasTuple_evaluation
   401	    (L : LdParams) {iota : Type*} [Fintype iota] [DecidableEq iota]
   402	    (G : DirectPolyMeasTuple L.toDirectLdParams
   403	      (iota × Fin (L.q / L.m))) (u : Fin L.m → ScalarQ L) :
   404	    (seedFiberCompressPolyMeasTuple L G).postprocess (evalPolyTupleAt u) =
   405	      seedFiberCompressMeasurement L
   406	        (G.postprocess (evalDirectPolyTupleAt u)) := by
   407	  exact (seedFiberCompressMeasurement_postprocess L G
   408	    (evalDirectPolyTupleAt u)).symm
   409	
   410	/-- Block-diagonal assembly commutes with deterministic outcome
   411	postprocessing. -/
   412	theorem blockDiagonalMeasurement_postprocess
   413	    {alpha beta iota block : Type*}
   414	    [Fintype alpha] [DecidableEq alpha]
   415	    [Fintype beta] [DecidableEq beta]
   416	    [Fintype iota] [DecidableEq iota]
   417	    [Fintype block] [DecidableEq block]
   418	    (M : block → MIPStarRE.Quantum.Measurement alpha iota)
   419	    (f : alpha → beta) :
   420	    (blockDiagonalMeasurement M).postprocess f =
   421	      blockDiagonalMeasurement (fun r => (M r).postprocess f) := by
   422	  classical
   423	  apply MIPStarRE.Quantum.Measurement.ext
   424	  intro b
   425	  ext ⟨i, r⟩ ⟨j, s⟩
   426	  simp only [MIPStarRE.Quantum.Measurement.postprocess_effect,
   427	    blockDiagonalMeasurement_effect, Matrix.sum_apply,
   428	    Matrix.blockDiagonal_apply]
   429	  by_cases hrs : r = s
   430	  · subst s
   431	    simp only [if_pos]
   432	  · simp [hrs]
   433	
   434	private theorem matrixMeasurementTransport_eq_postprocess
   435	    {alpha beta iota : Type*}
   436	    [Fintype alpha] [DecidableEq alpha]
   437	    [Fintype beta] [DecidableEq beta]
   438	    [Fintype iota] [DecidableEq iota]
   439	    (e : alpha ≃ beta) (M : MIPStarRE.Quantum.Measurement alpha iota) :
   440	    matrixMeasurementTransport e M = M.postprocess e := by
   441	  classical
   442	  apply MIPStarRE.Quantum.Measurement.ext
   443	  intro b
   444	  rw [MIPStarRE.Quantum.Measurement.postprocess_effect]
   445	  rw [Finset.sum_eq_single (e.symm b)]
   446	  · simp
   447	  · intro a haMem ha
   448	    have hea : e a = b := (Finset.mem_filter.mp haMem).2
   449	    exact (ha (e.injective (hea.trans (e.apply_symm_apply b).symm))).elim
   450	  · simp
   451	
   452	/-- Relabeling along an outcome equivalence commutes with subsequent
   453	postprocessing. -/
   454	theorem matrixMeasurementTransport_postprocess
   455	    {alpha beta gamma iota : Type*}
   456	    [Fintype alpha] [DecidableEq alpha]
   457	    [Fintype beta] [DecidableEq beta]
   458	    [Fintype gamma] [DecidableEq gamma]
   459	    [Fintype iota] [DecidableEq iota]
   460	    (e : alpha ≃ beta) (M : MIPStarRE.Quantum.Measurement alpha iota)
   461	    (f : beta → gamma) :
   462	    (matrixMeasurementTransport e M).postprocess f =
   463	      M.postprocess (fun a => f (e a)) := by
   464	  rw [matrixMeasurementTransport_eq_postprocess,
   465	    MIPStarRE.Quantum.Measurement.postprocess_comp]
   466	
   467	end
   468	
   469	end MIPStarRE.QPBT

    31	/-- The direct single-coordinate point/global defect is exactly the LDT
    32	defect after the polynomial, point, and scalar equivalences. -/
    33	theorem directPointPolynomial_consistencyDefect_eq
    34	    (D : DirectLdParams) (S : Strategy (directLdGame D))
    35	    (hS : S.IsProjective) (r : Fin D.k) :
    36	    letI := D.toLDTFieldModel
    37	    ∀ (G : ProjMeas (MIPStarRE.LDT.Polynomial D.toLDTParameters) S.ιB),
    38	      consistencyDefect
    39	          (uniformDistribution (Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D))
    40	          (fun u a => heteroKron
    41	            ((directPointCoordinateMeasurementA D S r u).effect a) 1)
    42	          (fun u a => heteroKron 1
    43	            ((directPolynomialEvaluationMeasurement D G u).effect a)) S.ψ =
    44	        consistencyDefect (uniformDistribution (Point D.toLDTParameters))
    45	          (ldtPointAPlaced D S hS r)
    46	          (ldtPolynomialEvaluationRight D G) S.ψ := by
    47	  letI := D.toLDTFieldModel
    48	  intro G
    49	  calc
    50	    consistencyDefect
    51	        (uniformDistribution (Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D))
    52	        (fun u a => heteroKron
    53	          ((directPointCoordinateMeasurementA D S r u).effect a) 1)
    54	        (fun u a => heteroKron 1
    55	          ((directPolynomialEvaluationMeasurement D G u).effect a)) S.ψ =
    56	      consistencyDefect
    57	        (uniformDistribution (Fin D.m → DirectScalarQ D))
    58	        (fun u a => ldtPointAPlaced D S hS r
    59	          (directPointEquiv D u) (directScalarEquiv D a))
    60	        (fun u a => ldtPolynomialEvaluationRight D G
    61	          (directPointEquiv D u) (directScalarEquiv D a)) S.ψ := by
    62	          apply consistencyDefect_congr
    63	          · intro u a
    64	            unfold ldtPointAPlaced
    65	            congr 1
    66	            exact (directCoordinatePointMeasurement_effect_transport
    67	              D S hS r u a).symm
    68	          · intro u a
    69	            unfold ldtPolynomialEvaluationRight
    70	            congr 1
    71	            exact directPolynomialMeasurement_evaluation_effect D G u a
    72	    _ = consistencyDefect (uniformDistribution (Point D.toLDTParameters))
    73	        (ldtPointAPlaced D S hS r)
    74	        (ldtPolynomialEvaluationRight D G) S.ψ :=
    75	      consistencyDefect_uniform_question_outcome_equiv
    76	        (directPointEquiv D) (directScalarEquiv D)
    77	        (ldtPointAPlaced D S hS r)

    30	@[simp] theorem seededLdQuestion_directLdPointQuestionOf
    31	    (L : LdParams) (u : Fin L.m → ScalarQ L)
    32	    (residue : Fin (L.q / L.m)) :

    41	    (L : LdParams) (a : DirectLdAnswer L.toDirectLdParams) :

    46	private theorem seedFiberPointMeasurement
    47	    (L : LdParams) {iota : Type*} [Fintype iota] [DecidableEq iota]

    51	    (blockDiagonalMeasurement fun residue =>
    52	        matrixMeasurementTransport (ldDirectAnswerEquiv L)

    54	            (directLdPointQuestionOf L.toDirectLdParams u) residue))).postprocess

    56	      blockDiagonalMeasurement fun _ =>

    60	  funext residue

    62	    seededLdQuestion_directLdPointQuestionOf]

    67	/-- The point POVM of the correlated-residue extension of the strategy is the

    69	theorem ldStrategyToDirect_pointMeasurementA

   102	    {iotaA iotaB block : Type*}
   103	    [Fintype iotaA] [DecidableEq iotaA]
   104	    [Fintype iotaB] [DecidableEq iotaB]
   105	    [Fintype block] [DecidableEq block] [Nonempty block]
   106	    (psi : EuclideanSpace ℂ (iotaA × iotaB))
   107	    (phi : EuclideanSpace ℂ ((iotaA × block) × (iotaB × block)))
   108	    (hphi : ∀ i j r s, phi ((i, r), (j, s)) =
   109	      if r = s then
   110	        psi (i, j) * (Real.sqrt (Fintype.card block : ℝ) : ℂ)⁻¹
   111	      else 0)
   112	    (A : Op (iotaA × block)) (B : Op iotaB) :
   113	    DistanceCalculus.stateQForm phi
   114	        (heteroKron A (Matrix.blockDiagonal fun _ => B)) =
   115	      DistanceCalculus.stateQForm psi
   116	        (heteroKron (averageDiagonalBlock A) B) := by
   117	  classical
   118	  unfold DistanceCalculus.stateQForm
   119	  apply congrArg Complex.re
   120	  unfold applyOperatorToState heteroKron Matrix.kronecker averageDiagonalBlock
   121	  simp_rw [EuclideanSpace.inner_eq_star_dotProduct]
   122	  simp only [Matrix.toEuclideanLin, Matrix.toLpLin_apply, dotProduct,
   123	    Matrix.mulVec]
   124	  simp_rw [← Finset.univ_product_univ, Finset.sum_product]
   125	  suffices h :
   126	      (∑ i : iotaA, ∑ r : block, ∑ j : iotaB,
   127	        ∑ i' : iotaA, ∑ j' : iotaB,
   128	          (starRingEnd ℂ)
   129	              (Real.sqrt (Fintype.card block : ℝ) : ℂ)⁻¹ *
   130	            (starRingEnd ℂ) (psi (i, j)) *
   131	              (B j j' * (A (i, r) (i', r) *
   132	                ((Real.sqrt (Fintype.card block : ℝ) : ℂ)⁻¹ *

   138	                ((Fintype.card block : ℂ)⁻¹ * A (i, r) (i', r)))) by
   139	    simpa [hphi, Matrix.blockDiagonal_apply, Matrix.kroneckerMap_apply,
   140	      apply_ite, map_zero, ite_mul, zero_mul, Finset.sum_ite_eq,

   142	      Matrix.sum_apply, Matrix.of_apply, Finset.mul_sum, Finset.sum_mul,
   143	      mul_assoc, mul_comm] using h
   144	  apply Fintype.sum_congr
   145	  intro i
   146	  rw [Finset.sum_comm]
   147	  apply Fintype.sum_congr
   148	  intro j
   149	  rw [Finset.sum_comm]
   150	  apply Fintype.sum_congr
   151	  intro i'
   152	  rw [Finset.sum_comm]
   153	  apply Fintype.sum_congr
   154	  intro j'
   155	  apply Fintype.sum_congr
   156	  intro r
   157	  ring_nf

   159	  ring

160	Thus, it will be convenient to introduce the following notation.
   161	Let $(\psi, A, B, L)$ be a symmetric strategy for the $(m+1, q, d)$-low individual degree test,
   162	Then for each $u \in \F_q^m$ we will write $B^u_f$ as shorthand for $B^{\ell}_f$,
   163	where $\ell = \{(u, x) \mid x \in \F_q\}$.
   164	For a function $f:\ell \rightarrow \F_q$,
   165	we will also sometimes write $f(x)$ as shorthand for $f(u,x)$.
   166	\end{notation}
   167	
   168	\begin{definition}
   169	Consider the $(m,q,d)$-low individual degree test.
   170	For $j \in \{1, \ldots, m\}$,
   171	we refer to the \emph{$j$-restricted diagonal lines test}
   172	as the diagonal lines test conditioned on $\bi = j$.
   173	For example, in the $m$-restricted diagonal lines test,
   174	the line $\bell$ is simply a uniformly random line in $\F_q^m$.
   175	\end{definition}
   176	
   177	Now we state our main theorem using notation which will be introduced in \Cref{sec:prelims} below.
   178	This the formal version of \Cref{thm:main-informal}.
   179	
   180	\begin{theorem}[Main theorem; quantum soundness of the low individual degree test]\label{thm:main-formal}
   181	  Consider a projective strategy $(\psi, A^{\mathrm{A}},B^{\mathrm{A}},L^{\mathrm{A}},A^{\mathrm{B}},B^{\mathrm{B}},L^{\mathrm{B}})$ 
   182	   which passes the  $(m,q,d)$-low individual degree test with probability at least $1-\eps$.
   183	  Let $k \geq md$ be an integer.
   184	  Let
   185	  \begin{equation*}
   186	  \nu = 100000 k^2m^4 \cdot \Big(\eps^{1/40000} + (d/q)^{1/40000} + e^{-k/(2560000m^2)}\Big).
   187	  \end{equation*}
   188	Then there exists projective measurements $G^{\mathrm{A}}, G^{\mathrm{B}} \in \polymeas{m}{q}{d}$ with the following properties:
   189	\begin{enumerate}
   190	  \item (Consistency with~$A$):  On average over $\bu \sim \F_q^{m}$,
   191		  \begin{align*}
   192		  A^{\mathrm{A},u}_a \otimes I
   193		  	&\simeq_{\nu} I \otimes G^{\mathrm{B}}_{[g(u)=a]},\\
   194		I \otimes A^{\mathrm{B},u}_a
   195		  	&\simeq_{\nu}  G^{\mathrm{A}}_{[g(u)=a]} \ot I.
   196		  \end{align*}
   197	\item (Self-consistency):
   198		\begin{equation*}
   199		G^{\mathrm{A}}_g \ot I \simeq_{\nu} I \ot G^{\mathrm{B}}_g.
   200		\end{equation*}
   201	\end{enumerate}
   202	\end{theorem}
   203	
   204	We note that there is a tradeoff in \Cref{thm:main-formal} specified by the parameter~$k$.
   205	As~$k$ increases, $\nu$'s prefactor $k^2$ increases.
   206	On the other hand, as $k$ increases, the term $e^{- k/(2560000m^2)}$ which also occurs in $\nu$ \emph{decreases}.
   207	Thus, when applying this theorem, one must select~$k$ to balance these competing demands.
   208	Typically, choosing $k = \poly(m)$ should be more than sufficient for applications.
   209	We believe that this parameter~$k$ is an artifact of our proof,
   210	and we hope that it will be removed in the future.
   211	
   385	    \end{enumerate}

   394	We define a special class of measurements that are relevant to the soundness
   395	properties of the low-degree test.
   396	
   397	\begin{definition}[Low-degree polynomial measurements]
   398	  \label{def:ld-meas}
   399	  Define $\polymeas{m}{d}{q}$ to be the set of POVM measurements whose outcomes
   400	  correspond to (individual) degree-$d$ polynomials of $m$ variables over
   401	  $\F_q$.
   402	  More generally, for an integer $\ldc$ and tuples $m=(m_1, m_2, \ldots,
   403	  m_\ldc)$, $d=(d_1, d_2, \ldots, d_\ldc)$ and $q=(q_1, q_2, \ldots, q_\ldc)$,
   404	  we let $\simulpolymeas{m}{d}{q}{\ldc}$ be the set of measurements $G =
   405	  \{G_{g_1,\, g_2,\, \ldots\,,\, g_\ldc}\}$ such that for $i\in\{1, 2, \ldots,
   406	  \ldc\}$, $g_i$ is a polynomial $g_i:\F_{q_i}^{m_i} \rightarrow
   407	  \F_{q_i}$ with individual degree $d_i$ (see \Cref{sec:ld-encoding} for a definition of individual degree). 
   408	\end{definition}
   409	
   410	Quantum soundness of a version of the classical low-degree test for polynomials of low \emph{total} degree was claimed
   411	in~\cite{natarajan2018low}, building on an analysis of a three-prover version of the test in~\cite{vidick2016three}. Unfortunately there is a gap in the soundness analysis of this test. For our construction we use the low individual degree test, whose quantum soundness is shown in~\cite{ML20} and generalized in~\cite{ji2021quantum}. We state the result in the form that is most directly useful for us, and show how the stated result follows from~\cite{ji2021quantum}.
   412	
   413	\begin{theorem}[Quantum soundness of the simultaneous classical low-degree test]
   414	  \label{lem:ld-soundness}
   415	  There exists a function $\delta_{\ld}(\eps, q, m, d, \ldc) = a (dm \ldc)^a (\eps^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bmd})$ for universal constants $a\geq 1$ and $0<b\leq 1$ 
   416	such that the following
   417	  holds.
   418	  For all $\eps > 0$ and parameter tuple $\ldparams = (q, m, d, \ldc)$, for all
   419	  projective strategies $(\psi,A,B)$ that succeed with probability at least
   420	  $1-\eps$ in the game $\game^\ld_\ldparams$, there exists measurements
   421	  \[G^w \in \simulpolymeas{m}{d}{q}{\ldc}\] on $\mH_w$, for
   422	  $w\in\{\alice,\bob\}$, such that
   423	  \begin{equation*}
   424	    \begin{split}
   425	      A^{\Point,\, u}_{a_1,\, a_2,\, \ldots\,,\, a_\ldc}
   426	      & \abc[\delta_{\ld}]
   427	      G^\bob_{[(g_1(u),g_2(u),\ldots,g_\ldc(u)) = (a_1,\, a_2,\, \ldots \,,\, a_\ldc)]}\;,\\
   428	      G^\alice_{[(g_1(u),g_2(u),\ldots,g_\ldc(u)) = (a_1,\, a_2,\, \ldots \,,\, a_\ldc)]}
   429	      & \abc[\delta_{\ld}]
   430				 B^{\Point,\, u}_{a_1,\, a_2,\, \ldots\,,\, a_\ldc}\;,\\
   431	      G^\alice_{g_1,\, g_2,\, \ldots \,,\, g_\ldc}
   432	      & \abc[\delta_{\ld}]
   433	      G^\bob_{g_1,\, g_2,\, \ldots \,,\, g_\ldc}\;,
   434	    \end{split}
   435	  \end{equation*}
   436	  where $\delta_{\ld} = \delta_{\ld}(\eps, q, m, d, \ldc)$, 
   437	  and all three statements are with respect to the state $\ket{\psi}$.
   438	In addition, the first two approximations hold under the uniform distribution over $u\in \F_q^m$,
   439		whereas there is no question distribution associated with the third approximation.
   440	\end{theorem}
   441	
   442	\begin{proof}
   443	Let $\ldparams = (q, m, d, \ldc)$
   444	where $m, d, \ldc \in \N$ are integers, $q \in \N$ is an admissible field size,
   445	and $m$ divides $q$. Let $\Sigma=\F_q$. Let $\code \subseteq \Sigma^q$ be the Reed-Solomon code with degree $d$. Explicitly, $\code$ is the set of all $(p(x_1),\ldots,p(x_n))$ where $p:\F_q\to\F_q$ is a univariate polynomial of degree at most $d$ and $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ are an enumeration of $\F_q$. Then in the (standard) notation from~\cite{ji2021quantum} $\code$ is a linear $[q,d+1,n-d+1]_\Sigma$ code.
   446	
   447	Observe that the two-prover tensor code test, for the code $\code^{\otimes m}$, as described in~\cite[Figure 1 and Figure 2]{ji2021quantum}, is identical to the game $\game^\ld$ with parameters $\ldparams$ and $\ldc=1$, whose decider is presented in Figure~\ref{fig:ld-decider}. This is because 
   448	\begin{enumerate}
   449	\item The \emph{axis-parallel line-versus-point test} from Figure~\ref{fig:ld-decider} is identical to the \emph{axis-parallel lines test} from~\cite[Figure 1]{ji2021quantum}, with the only difference that in Figure~\ref{fig:ld-decider} the roles of A and B are chosen uniformly at random. This is consistent with the two-prover variant of the tensor code test from~\cite[Section 4.1]{ji2021quantum}.
   450	\item The \emph{diagonal line-versus-point test} from Figure~\ref{fig:ld-decider} is identical to the \emph{subcube commutation test} from~\cite[Figure 1]{ji2021quantum}, with again the added symmetrization between players. 
   451	\item The \emph{consistency test} from Figure~\ref{fig:ld-decider} is identical to the \emph{synchronicity test} from~\cite[Figure 2]{ji2021quantum}.
   452	\end{enumerate}
   453	
   454	As a result,~\cite[Theorem 4.7]{ji2021quantum}, in which we choose the parameter $k$ as $k=m^3d$,  immediately yields \Cref{lem:ld-soundness}.
   455	
   456	To conclude it remains to extend the result to the case of general $\ldc$. This is done 
   457	via a standard reduction, following exactly the same steps as the derivation of Theorem 4.43 from Theorem 4.40 in~\cite{NW19}.
   458	\end{proof}

   265	/-- Evaluation of a coefficient tuple at a field element.  This is the

   272	  ∑ i : Fin n, c i * t ^ i.val
   273	
   274	/-- Check that an answer has the constructor prescribed by its question type;
   275	Lean encoding of the rejection clause in `def:ld-win-predicate`, blueprint

   277	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.

   282	  | .aline, .alinePolys _ => true
   283	  | .dline, .dlinePolys _ => true

   285	
   286	/-- The axis-parallel line/point relation in `def:ld-win-predicate`, blueprint
   287	`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:56-105`, paper origin
   288	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.

   291	    (f : Fin P.k → Fin (P.d + 1) → ScalarQ P)
   292	    (a : Fin P.k → ScalarQ P) : Prop :=
   293	  -- Universal quantification follows the zero-direction convention in
   294	  -- `rem:ld-win-zero-direction`.
   295	  ∀ t : ScalarQ P,
   296	    point.point = line.point + t • coordinateDirection (chiIndex P line.seed) →
   297	      ∀ j : Fin P.k, evalCoefficient (f j) t = a j
   298	
   299	/-- The diagonal line/point relation in `def:ld-win-predicate`, blueprint
   300	`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:56-105`, paper origin
   301	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.
   302	-/
   303	def dlinePointCondition (P : LdParams) (line point : LdSpace P)
   304	    (f : Fin P.k → Fin (P.m * P.d + 1) → ScalarQ P)
   305	    (a : Fin P.k → ScalarQ P) : Prop :=
   306	  ∀ t : ScalarQ P,
   307	    point.point = line.point + t • line.direction →
   308	      ∀ j : Fin P.k, evalCoefficient (f j) t = a j
   309	
   310	/-- The low-degree consistency predicate, rejecting answers of the wrong
   311	constructor shape.  This is `def:ld-win-predicate` in
   312	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:56-105`, paper origin
   313	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.
   314	-/
   315	noncomputable def ldWinPredicate (P : LdParams) :
   316	    LdQuestion P → LdQuestion P → LdAnswer P → LdAnswer P → Bool :=
   317	  open Classical in
   318	  fun (tA, xA) (tB, xB) a b =>
   319	      if validLdAnswer tA a && validLdAnswer tB b then
   320	        match tA, tB, a, b with
   321	        | .point, .point, .pointVals u, .pointVals v => decide (u = v)
   322	        | .aline, .point, .alinePolys f, .pointVals u =>
   323	            decide (alinePointCondition P xA xB f u)
   324	        | .point, .aline, .pointVals u, .alinePolys f =>
   325	            decide (alinePointCondition P xB xA f u)
   326	        | .dline, .point, .dlinePolys f, .pointVals u =>
   327	            decide (dlinePointCondition P xA xB f u)
   328	        | .point, .dline, .pointVals u, .dlinePolys f =>
   329	            decide (dlinePointCondition P xB xA f u)
   330	        | .aline, .aline, .alinePolys f, .alinePolys g => decide (f = g)
   331	        | .dline, .dline, .dlinePolys f, .dlinePolys g => decide (f = g)
   332	        | _, _, _, _ => true
   333	      else false

   335	/-- The low-degree game packaged as a `Game`.  This is `def:ld-game` in
   336	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:17-105`, paper origin
   337	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.

   339	noncomputable def ldGame (P : LdParams) : Game where

   124	There, the combined point measurements

   126	$\{\hat Q^{\ell}_f\}$, indexed by points of $\F_q^{2m+2}$ and lines in

   138	The game, however, is parametrized by tuples $(q,m',d,k)$ with $q$ an
   139	admissible field size \emph{and $m'$ dividing $q$}.  The divisibility is not

1	\section{Classical and Quantum Low-degree Tests}
     2	\label{sec:ldt}
     3	
     4	In this section we introduce the classical and quantum low individual degree tests, that form the basis of our classical, quantum-sound and quantum PCP constructions. For quantum soundness of the classical test we refer to~\cite{ML20}. For the quantum test, we refer to~\cite{natarajan2018low} and its adaptation to the low individual degree test given in Appendix~\ref{sec:qld-analysis}. 
     5	The protocol in this work combines both of these tests, using the quantum
     6	low individual degree test for question reduction and the classical low individual degree test for
     7	answer reduction.
     8	Section~\ref{sec:ld-verifier} below introduces the classical test,
     9	and Section~\ref{sec:pauli-verifier} does the same for the quantum 
    10	test.
    11	Prior to doing this, we introduce the \emph{Magic Square game} in
    12	Section~\ref{sec:ms}, a key subroutine in the quantum test.
    13	
    14	
    15	\subsection{The classical low-degree test}
    16	\label{sec:ld-verifier}
    17	
    18	We begin with a generalization of the classical low-degree test known as the
    19	``simultaneous individual low-degree test''.
    20	We sometimes refer to this as the ``classical low-degree test'' for short.
    21	The low-degree test is used as a subroutine in the Pauli Basis test (see
    22	Section~\ref{sec:pauli-verifier}) as well as the answer-reduction normal form
    23	verifier (see Section~\ref{sec:ans}).
    24	We describe the test as a nonlocal game in Section~\ref{sec:ld-game} and show
    25	that the question distribution can be implemented as a (typed) conditionally
    26	linear distribution (see \Cref{sec:types} for the definition of typed CL
    27	distributions).
    28	
    29	
    30	\subsubsection{The game}
    31	\label{sec:ld-game}
    32	
    33	The game $\game^\ld$ is parametrized by a tuple $\ldparams = (q, m, d, \ldc)$
    34	where $m, d, \ldc \in \N$ are integers, $q \in \N$ is an admissible field size,
    35	and $m$ divides $q$.
    36	We sometimes write $\game^\ld_\ldparams$ to emphasize the dependence of the
    37	classical low-degree test on the parameter tuple $\ldparams$.
    38	
    39	We first provide a high-level description of the game for $k=1$.
    40	It is based on the low-individual degree variant of the multilinearity test
    41	of~\cite{babai1991non}, where one player (called the ``points player'') receives
    42	a random point $u \in \F_q^m$, and the other player (called the ``lines
    43	player'') receives a random axis-parallel line $\line$ that contains $u$, i.e.\
    44	the line parallel to the $i$-th axis which goes through point $u$, for uniformly
    45	random $i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$.
    46	The points player is supposed to respond with a value $a \in \F_q$, and the
    47	lines player is supposed to respond with a univariate polynomial $f_\line$ of
    48	degree at most $d$ such that $f_\line(u_i) = a$, where $u_i$ is the $i$-th
    49	coordinate of $u$.
    50	
    51	Suppose the players agree beforehand on a global polynomial $g: \F_q^m \to \F_q$
    52	such that every variable has degree at most $d$.
    53	Then a winning strategy is the following: the points player responds with
    54	$g(u)$, and the lines player responds with the univariate polynomial $f_\line$
    55	that is the restriction of $g$ to line $\line$; formally, for $t \in \F_q$,
    56	\[f_\line(t)=g(u_1,u_2,\ldots,u_{i-1},t,u_{i+1},\ldots,u_m)\;.\] It is easy to
    57	see that $f_\line(t)$ has degree at most $d$ in the variable $t$.
    58	Thus in this case the players will pass the low-degree test with probability
    59	$1$.
    60	The low-degree testing theorem states that the converse approximately holds: if
    61	the players pass the low-degree test with probability close to $1$, then their
    62	responses must be approximately consistent (in some sense) with a global
    63	polynomial $g$ with individual degree $d$.
    64	
    65	When $k > 1$, the players are supposed to respond with a \emph{tuple} of
    66	answers; and the test is intended to check that the players' responses are
    67	consistent with a $k$-tuple of functions $g_i: \F_q^m \to \F_q$ that are
    68	polynomials where every variable has degree at most $d$.
    69	
    70	The game that we use is slightly more elaborate than the ``axis-parallel
    71	lines-versus-points'' test just described.
    72	In addition, we have two other subtests.
    73	One is a ``diagonal line-vs-points'' test: here, the points player receives a
    74	point $u \in \F_q^m$ as before, but the lines player receives a line $\line$
    75	that goes through $u$ but is not necessarily axis-aligned.
    76	Instead, it's chosen by first picking an index $i \in \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$
    77	uniformly at random, picking $v \in \F_q^m$ uniformly at random, and letting $v'
    78	= \pi_{i-1}(v) = (0,0,\ldots,0,v_i,v_{i+1},\ldots,v_m)$ (i.e., $\pi_{i-1}$
    79	zeroes out the first $i-1$ coordinates of its input).
    80	Then, the line is defined as the set
    81	\[
    82		\line = \{ u + tv' : t \in \F_q \}\;,
    83	\]
    84	which is a uniformly random line in the affine subspace of $\F^m_q$
    85	corresponding to all points $v$ whose first $(i-1)$ coordinates match those of
    86	$u$.
    87	The points player responds with a value $a \in \F_q$, the lines player responds
    88	with a univariate polynomial $f_\line$ of degree $md$,\footnote{Since $\line$ is
    89	  no longer axis-parallel, the restriction of an individual degree-$d$
    90	  polynomial $g$ to a line $\line$ may yield a degree $md$ polynomial.}
    91	and the verifier checks that $f_\line(t_u) = a$ (where $t_u \in \F_q$ is the
    92	projection of $u$ onto the line $\line$ with respect to a canonical
    93	parameterization of $\line$).
    94	
    95	The other additional test is a ``consistency test'', where both players receive
    96	either the same points question, the same axis-parallel lines question, or the
    97	same diagonal lines question.
    98	In all cases they are expected to respond with the same answer.
    99	
   100	
   101	
   102	\paragraph{Axis-parallel lines and diagonal lines.}
   103	Before presenting a formal description of the game $\game^\ld$, we first define
   104	what we mean by lines, and their properties.
   105	
   106	\begin{definition}[Lines]
   107	  \label{def:line}
   108		A \emph{line} $\line$ in $\F^m_q$ specified by a pair $(u,v) \in (\F_q^m)^2$
   109	  is the subset
   110	  \begin{equation}
   111	    \label{eq:line-set}
   112	    \line(u,v) = \bigl\{\, u + tv : t \in \F_q \,\bigr\} \subseteq \F_q^m \;.
   113	  \end{equation}
   114	  We call the vector $v$ a \emph{direction} of line
   115	  $\line(u,v)$.\footnote{For convenience we explicitly allow
   116	    $v=0$, in which case the line is reduced to a singleton.}
   117	  
   118	  A line $\line(u,v)$ is \emph{axis-parallel} if there is a coordinate $i \in
   119	  \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ for which $v$ is equal to $e_i$, the $i$-th elementary basis
   120	  vector in $\F_q^m$.
   121	  We say that such a line $\line$ is \emph{parallel to the $i$-th direction}.
   122	  A line $\line(u,v)$ is \emph{diagonal} if there exists an $i \in
   123	  \{0,1,\ldots,m-1\}$ for which $v_1 = v_2 = \cdots = v_i = 0$.
   124	\end{definition}
   125	
   126	The following Proposition establishes that, for a fixed direction, a line
   127	$\line$ is an equivalence class of points on the line.
   128	\begin{proposition}
   129	  \label{prop:line-equiv}
   130	  Let $u,v \in \F_q^m$.
   131	  Then for all $u' \in \line(u,v)$, we have that $\line(u,v) = \line(u',v)$.
   132	\end{proposition}
   133	\begin{proof}
   134		Fix $u' \in \line(u,v)$.
   135	  We have that $u' = u + tv$ for some $t \in \F_q$.
   136	  Let $a \in \line(u,v)$.
   137	  This means that $a = u + sv$ for some $s\in \F_q$.
   138	  We also have that $a = u + (s - t + t)v = u + tv + (s - t)v = u' + (s - t)v$,
   139	  so $\line(u,v) \subseteq \line(u',v)$.
   140	  A similar argument shows that $\line(u',v) \subseteq \line(u,v)$.
   141	\end{proof}
   142	
   143	We now specify a canonical representation of lines $\line = \line(u,v)$ as pairs $(u_0,v)$
   144	where $u_0$ is a \emph{canonical representative} of $\line$ specified as
   145	follows.
   146	Let $L_v^{\lnf}: \F_q^m \to \F_q^m$ denote the canonical linear map with the
   147	one-dimensional kernel basis $\{v\}$ (see \Cref{def:cl-canonical} for a
   148	definition of canonical linear map).
   149	Note that for all $u \in \line$, we have that $L_v^{\lnf}(u)$ is a point in
   150	$\line$.
   151	This is because since the image and kernel of $L_v^{\lnf}$ are complementary
   152	subspaces by definition (see \Cref{def:cl-canonical}), any $u \in \F_q^m$ has a
   153	unique decomposition $u = u_0 + u_1$ where $u_0$ is in the image of $L_v^{\lnf}$
   154	and $u_1 \in \ker(L_v^{\lnf})$, which by definition is the subspace spanned by
   155	$v$.
   156	Thus $u_1 = tv$ for some $t \in \F_q$ and we have that $u_0 = u - tv \in \line$.
   157	In particular, if $u\in \line$ then $u_0 = L_v^{\lnf}(u) \in \line$ as well. 
   158	Furthermore, since $L_v^{\lnf}$ is a projection onto its image by definition, we
   159	have $L_v^{\lnf}(u_0) = u_0$.
   160	
   160	
   161	Next, note that for any $u,u' \in \line$, since $u-u' = sv$ for some $s\in \F_q$
   162	it follows that $L_v^\lnf(u) = L_v^\lnf(u')$.
   163	Thus $u_0 = u_0'$ and this shows that $L_v^\lnf$ gives a means to compute a
   164	canonical representative of lines.
   165	
   166	\begin{definition}[Canonical representative of a line]
   167	  \label{def:line-representative}
   168	  Let $\line$ be a line in direction $v$.
   169	  A canonical representative of $\line$ is the point $u_0 \in \F_q^m$ such that
   170	  \[
   171	    u_0 = L_v^\lnf(u)
   172	  \]
   173	  for all $u \in \line$.
   174	\end{definition}
   175	
   176	
   177	
   178	\paragraph{Question distribution.}
   179	We now present the question distribution of the game $\game^\ld$ as a typed CL
   180	distribution (see \Cref{sec:types} for the definition of typed CL functions and
   181	typed CL distributions).
   182	The type set $\type^\ld$ of the game $\game^\ld$ we use is
   183	\[
   184		\type^\ld = \{ \Point, \ALine, \DLine \}\;.
   185	\]
   186	The distribution over question types is uniform over $\type^\ld \times \type^\ld$. 
   187	
   188	We introduce the corresponding typed CL functions $L_\Point$, $L_\ALine$,
   189	$L_\DLine$ where the corresponding CL distributions $\mu_{L_\ALine,L_\Point}$
   190	and $\mu_{L_\DLine,L_\Point}$ implement the axis line-versus-point and diagonal
   191	line-versus-point distributions, respectively.
   192	The functions are parametrized by a field size $q$, a dimension $m$, and three
   193	complementary register subspaces $V_\xpt,V_{\coord}, V_{\dir{}}$ of some ambient
   194	space.
   195	The register $V_\xpt$ (which is isomorphic to $\F_q^m$) is called the
   196	\emph{point register}, $V_\coord$ (which is isomorphic to $\F_q$) is called the
   197	\emph{coordinate register}, and $V_{\dir{}}$ (which is isomorphic to $\F_q^m$)
   198	is called the \emph{direction register}, respectively.
   199	We let $V$ denote the direct sum $V_\xpt \oplus V_{\coord} \oplus V_{\dir{}}$.
   200	We identify elements of $V$ as triples $(u,s,v) \in \F_q^m \times \F_q \times
   201	\F_q^m$.
   202	
   203	Define $L_\Point$ to be the $1$-level CL function that projects onto $V_\xpt$: for every $(u,s,v) \in V$,
   204	\begin{equation}
   205	  \label{eq:cl-ptf}
   206		L_\Point(u,s,v) = (u,0,0) \;.
   207	\end{equation}
   208	Define $L_\ALine$ to be the following $2$-level CL function:
   209	\begin{equation}
   210	  \label{eq:cl-alnf}
   211		L_\ALine(u,s,v) = (L^\lnf_{e_i}(u), s, 0)\ \text{for all } (u,s,v) \in V,
   212	\end{equation}
   213	where $L^\lnf$ is the linear function used to compute the canonical
   214	representative of lines (see \Cref{def:line-representative}), and $i = \chi(s)$
   215	where we define $\chi(s)$ to be the unique integer such that
   216	\begin{equation}
   217	\label{eq:chi-func}
   218		s = (\chi(s) - 1) \frac{q}{m} + r
   219	\end{equation}
   220	for some $0 \leq r < q/m$, and we interpret the field element $s \in \F_q$ as an
   221	integer between $0$ and $q - 1$).
   222	The function $L_\ALine$ is the concatenation of the $1$-level CL function that
   223	projects the subspaces $V_{\coord} \oplus V_{\dir{}}$ down to $V_\coord$ (i.e.
   224	zeroes out the entire $V_{\dir{}}$ register), and the family of $1$-level CL
   225	functions $\{L^\lnf_{e_i} \}$ acting on $V_\xpt$, indexed by $i \in
   226	\{1,2,\ldots,m\}$.
   227	(See \Cref{lem:cl-concat} for definition of CL function concatenation.)
   228	Thus $L_\ALine$ is a $2$-level CL function.
   229	
   230	Define $L_\DLine$ to be the following $3$-level CL function: for all $(u,s,v) \in
   231	V$,
   232	\begin{equation}
   233	\label{eq:cl-dlnf}
   234		L_\DLine(u,s,v) = (L^\lnf_{\pi_{i-1}(v)}(u),s,\pi_{i-1}(v))
   235	\end{equation}
   236	where $i = \chi(s)$.
   237	The function $L_\DLine$ is the concatenation of the following CL functions (again, see \Cref{lem:cl-concat} for definition of CL function concatenation): (i) the identity function on $V_{\coord}$ (which is a $1$-level CL function); (ii) for every $i \in \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ the $1$-level CL function on $V_{\dir{}}$ that maps $v \mapsto \pi_{i-1}(v)$ (i.e.~it zeroes out the first $i-1$ coordinates of $v$), and (iii) for every pair $(s,v') \in V_\coord \oplus V_{\dir{}}$, the $1$-level CL function $L^\lnf_{v'}$ acting on $V_\xpt$. Thus $L_\DLine$ is a $3$-level CL function.

   240	The following two lemmas establish that the CL functions
   241	$L_\Point,L_\ALine,L_\DLine$ give rise to the axis-parallel line-versus-point and
   242	diagonal line-versus-point distributions.
   243	\begin{lemma}
   244		\label{lem:alnf}
   245		Consider the pair $(\line, u)$ sampled in the following way: first, sample the
   246	  tuple $((u_0,s,0),(u,0,0))$ from the CL distribution $\mu_{L_\ALine,L_\Point}$,
   247	  and let $\line = \line(u_0,e_i)$ where $i = \chi(s)$.
   248	  Then $u$ is a uniformly random point in $\F_q^m$ and $\line$ is a line that
   249	  goes through $u$ and is parallel to a uniformly random axis $i \in
   250	  \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$.
   251	\end{lemma}
   252	\begin{proof}
   253		Since $s$ is uniformly random in $\F_q$ and $m$ divides $q$ by assumption, we
   254	  have that $i$ is uniformly random between $\{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ and therefore
   255	  $(u_0,s)$ specifies a uniformly random axis-parallel line $\line(u_0,e_i)$.
   256	  Since $u_0 = L^{\lnf}_{e_i}(u)$, we have that $u \in \line(u_0,e_i)$.
   257	\end{proof}
   258

   261	\begin{lemma}
   262		\label{lem:dlnf}
   263		Consider the pair $(\line,u)$ sampled in the following way: first, sample the
   264	  tuple $((u_0,s,v),(u,0,0))$ from the CL distribution $\mu_{L_\DLine,L_\Point}$,
   265	  and let $\line = \line(u_0,v)$ where $i = \chi(s)$.
   266	  Then $u$ is a uniformly random point in $\F_q^m$ and $\line$ is a random
   267	  diagonal line that goes through $u$ and shares the first $i-1$ coordinates
   268	  with $u$, for uniformly random $i$.
   269	\end{lemma}
   270	\begin{proof}
   271		The proof of this follows identically to \Cref{lem:alnf}.
   272	\end{proof}

   276	\begin{definition}[Line-point distributions]
   277	        \label{def:line-point-dist}
   278	 The \emph{axis line-point distribution} $D_{\ALine}$ is the
   279	 distribution $\mu_{L_\ALine,L_\Point}$ over pairs $(\ell=(u_0,e_i),u)$
   280	 (we omit the $0$ elements for simplicity). The \emph{diagonal
   281	   line-point distribution} $D_{\DLine}$ is the distribution
   282	 $\mu_{L_\DLine,L_\Point}$  over $(\ell=(u_0,s,v),u)$. The
   283	 \emph{line-point distribution} $D_{\Line}$ is the equal mixture of the axis-parallel line-point distribution and the diagonal line-point distribution.
   284	 In other words, a sample from $D_{\Line}$ is distributed as follows:
   285	 with probability $\tfrac{1}{2}$, output a sample from $D_{\ALine}$,
   286	 and with probability $\tfrac{1}{2}$, output a sample from $D_{\DLine}$.
   287	\end{definition}

   320	\paragraph{Decision procedure} The decision procedure $\decider^\ld$ for the
   321	game $\game^\ld$ is presented in Figure~\ref{fig:ld-decider}.
   322	The table at the top specifies a parsing scheme for the questions and answers,
   323	depending on the type of question.
   324	For example, when a player receives a question with type $\Point$, the question
   325	content $x$, a bit string of length $m \log q$, should be interpreted by the
   326	decision procedure and the players as an element of the vector space $\F_q^m$,
   327	as indicated in Section~\ref{sec:ff-representations}.
   328	Similarly the answer to a question with type $\Point$ is expected to be a bit
   329	string of length $\ldc \log q$, and is interpreted as an element of $\F_q^\ldc$.
   330	For questions with type $\ALine$, the question content is a $(m \log q + \log
   331	q)$-bit string, which is parsed as a pair $(u_0, s) \in \F_q^m \times \F_q$,
   332	which in turn can be interpreted as a specification for an axis-parallel line
   333	$\line(u_0,e_i)$ in $\F_q^m$ where $i = \chi(s)$, as described in
   334	\Cref{lem:alnf}.
   335	The answer is interpreted as the description of $\ldc$ degree-$d$ univariate
   336	polynomials defined on the line $\line(u_0,e_i)$, each polynomial given by a
   337	list of $d+1$ coefficients.
   338	For questions with type $\DLine$, the question content is a $(2m \log q + \log
   339	q)$-bit string, which is parsed as a triple $(u_0, s, v) \in \F_q^m \times \F_q
   340	\times \F_q^m$ that specifies a diagonal line $\line(u_0,v')$ where $v' =
   341	\pi_{i-1}(v)$ as described in \Cref{lem:dlnf}.
   342	The answer is interpreted as the description of $\ldc$ degree-$md$ univariate
   343	polynomials defined on the line $\line(u_0,v')$.
   344	If the answers returned by the players do not fit this format the decision
   345	procedure rejects.

   394	We define a special class of measurements that are relevant to the soundness
   395	properties of the low-degree test.
   396	
   397	\begin{definition}[Low-degree polynomial measurements]
   398	  \label{def:ld-meas}
   399	  Define $\polymeas{m}{d}{q}$ to be the set of POVM measurements whose outcomes
   400	  correspond to (individual) degree-$d$ polynomials of $m$ variables over
   401	  $\F_q$.
   402	  More generally, for an integer $\ldc$ and tuples $m=(m_1, m_2, \ldots,
   403	  m_\ldc)$, $d=(d_1, d_2, \ldots, d_\ldc)$ and $q=(q_1, q_2, \ldots, q_\ldc)$,
   404	  we let $\simulpolymeas{m}{d}{q}{\ldc}$ be the set of measurements $G =
   405	  \{G_{g_1,\, g_2,\, \ldots\,,\, g_\ldc}\}$ such that for $i\in\{1, 2, \ldots,
   406	  \ldc\}$, $g_i$ is a polynomial $g_i:\F_{q_i}^{m_i} \rightarrow
   407	  \F_{q_i}$ with individual degree $d_i$ (see \Cref{sec:ld-encoding} for a definition of individual degree). 
   408	\end{definition}

   256	\paragraph{Obligation 2: the parameter bound.}
   257	Theorem~4.7 requires $K \ge 12 m' t = 12 m' (d+1)$.  The source
   258	instantiates $K = (m')^3 d$, which meets the bound iff
   259	$(m')^2 d \ge 12(d+1)$: this holds for all $d \ge 1$ when $m' \ge 5$,
   260	holds at $m' = 4$ exactly when $d \ge 3$, and fails for every $d$ when
   261	$m' \le 3$.  In the game's parameter domain the dimension divides the
   262	admissible field size and is therefore a power of two, so the source's
   263	instantiation violates the hypothesis exactly at $m' \in \{1,2\}$ for
   264	every $d$ and at $m' = 4$ for $d \in \{1,2\}$ --- in particular, in the
   265	multilinear regime $d = 1$, at every dimension $m' \le 4$.  A candidate
   266	repair is to instantiate $K = \max((m')^3 d,\, 12 m'(d+1))$; the open
   267	obligation is then to re-absorb the error, that is, to check that
   268	$\mathrm{poly}(m',t,K)$ and $e^{-K/(m')^2}$ still collapse to the form
   269	$a(dm')^a(\eps^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bm'd})$ in the small-$m'$ cases where the
   270	maximum is $12m'(d+1)$ --- plausible, since there
   271	$e^{-K/(m')^2} = e^{-12(d+1)/m'}$ decays in $d$ at a rate comparable to
   272	$2^{-m'd}$ for $m' \le 4$, but not checked here.

   274	In the correspondence of Obligation~1, the only role of the divisibility
   275	$m' \mid q$ is to make the $\chi$-sampled index uniform.  The underlying
   276	mathematics does not need the divisibility.  The low
   277	individual degree test of \cite{Ji2020LowIndividualDegree} samples its axis
   278	index $i$ uniformly from $\{1,\ldots,m'\}$ directly, with no index function
   279	on $\F_q$ and no divisibility hypothesis,%
   280	\footnote{See the test figure in \path{references/ldt-paper/test_definition.tex}.}
   281	and the tensor-code test is likewise a test about the code
   282	$\mathcal C^{\ot m'}$, not about an encoding of indices into $\F_q$.  The
   283	$\chi$-based packaging exists so that the question distribution is
   284	conditionally linear, which the introspection machinery requires for the
   285	game the players actually play --- the Pauli basis test at dimension $m$,

   287	$2m+2$ never appears in a verifier; it is an internal analysis device in the
   288	proof of the polynomial-pair lemma, so nothing there requires its question
